quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: files vs. databases

questions.scenarioTitle: The address that only half-changed
questions.stem: Access Pet Center moves to a new building. KimTay's front office updates the address in customer_list.xlsx, but nobody touches invoices_2026.docx, which still prints the old street. Using the four problems named in this lesson, which one has that missed update just created?
options: Data redundancy, because the address was written into more than one file in the first place
Data isolation, because the address sits in files that different departments happen to own
Data inconsistency, because two files now disagree about the same customer's address
Limited sharing and security, because the front office edited a file the billing clerk also uses
optionNotes: Redundancy was already there before anyone moved - it is the pre-existing condition that made this failure possible, not the new problem the missed update created.
Isolation is about being unable to combine data from separate files; here the address can be found in both files, it just disagrees.
Correct - the lesson defines data inconsistency as one copy getting updated while the others do not, so different files disagree about the same fact.
Sharing and security is about who is allowed to open or change a file; nobody's permissions caused this, a missed update did.
questions.takeaway: Redundancy is storing the same fact twice; inconsistency is what happens when one of those copies is updated and the others are not.

questions.scenarioTitle: The question nobody could answer
questions.stem: Before the database, KimTay's owner asked, 'Which of Valerie Kaiser's customers ordered anything in June?' Rep assignments lived in rep_commissions.xlsx, customer details in customer_list.xlsx, and orders in invoices_2026.docx, with no shared code linking them. Which of the lesson's four file-system problems does this show?
options: Data isolation, because related data sits in separate, incompatible files that cannot easily be combined
Data inconsistency, because three different files all hold information about the same June orders
Data redundancy, because answering the question means reading the same customer name three times
Limited sharing and security, because the owner does not have permission to open the sales files
optionNotes: Correct - the lesson calls this data isolation: related data scattered across incompatible files makes questions that span more than one file hard to answer.
Inconsistency means the files actually disagree about a fact; nothing here says any file is wrong, only that they cannot be joined up.
Redundancy is about storing one fact more than once and wasting space; the owner's trouble is pulling facts together, not storing them.
The lesson's sharing and security problem is about weak control over who may see or change files; the owner can open all three, he just cannot connect them.
questions.takeaway: When a question needs data from more than one file and nothing links those files, the problem is data isolation.

questions.scenarioTitle: What exactly did we just buy?
questions.stem: KimTay decides to move off spreadsheets. A consultant installs MySQL on the office server, then loads the `REP`, `CUSTOMER`, `ITEM`, `INVOICE`, and `INVOICE_LINE` tables into it. In this course's vocabulary, what is MySQL?
options: The database itself, since the word database means the software that stores KimTay's data
One very large file that replaces customer_list.xlsx one for one
A reporting tool that prints the tables, so KimTay still needs its old files to store them
The DBMS - the software layer that creates, secures, and manages the database of tables
optionNotes: The database is the structured, shared collection of related tables; MySQL is the software that manages it, which this lesson calls the DBMS.
A database is not one big file - it is a set of related tables, and the DBMS is separate software that manages all of them at once.
A DBMS does far more than print: it creates, secures, and manages the stored data itself, so the old files are not needed at all.
Correct - the lesson names MySQL, Oracle, and Microsoft Access as examples of a DBMS, the software that lets people create, read, update, and delete data safely.
questions.takeaway: The database is the data; the DBMS - MySQL, Oracle, Access - is the software that manages it.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: the KimTay tables

questions.scenarioTitle: Whiskers and Wags gets a new rep
questions.stem: Customer 1420, Whiskers & Wags Boutique, is currently assigned to rep 65, Juan Perez. KimTay reassigns the account to rep 35, Richard Hull. Using the design walked through in Lesson 1-2, what is the correct edit?
options: Add a new row to `REP` for Richard Hull, so he has one row for each customer he handles
Change `REP_NUM` from 65 to 35 in the single `CUSTOMER` row for 1420, and nothing else
Copy Hull's last name, city, and commission rate onto customer 1420's row so reports can read them
Edit the `REP_NUM` stored on every `INVOICE` row that belongs to customer 1420
optionNotes: `REP` holds one row per sales representative, not one row per customer; Hull already has his row, number 35.
Correct - `CUSTOMER.REP_NUM` is a foreign key holding only the rep's number, so reassigning the account is a one-value change in one row.
Copying Hull's details onto the customer row recreates the exact redundancy this design exists to avoid; the foreign key already reaches that data.
`INVOICE` stores only `CUSTOMER_NUM` and has no `REP_NUM` column at all - the rep is reached through the customer.
questions.takeaway: A foreign key means changing a relationship is one small value change, never a copy of the other table's data.

questions.scenarioTitle: The intern who wanted one less table
questions.stem: An intern argues that `INVOICE_LINE` is unnecessary: just put an `ITEM_ID` column on `INVOICE`. But invoice 50712 already carries two items, AV07 and FT88, and item CF21 appears on invoice 50710 and again on invoice 50711. Why does the intern's idea fail?
options: `ITEM_ID` is text and `INVOICE_NUM` is a number, so the two cannot be stored in the same table
It works fine as long as both item codes are typed into that one column separated by commas
Items never need to be recorded on an order at all, because `ITEM` already stores every item's price
One column holds only one item code per invoice, so a table with one row per invoice-and-item pairing is needed
optionNotes: Tables routinely mix text and number columns; `ITEM_ID` and `INVOICE_NUM` already sit side by side inside `INVOICE_LINE`.
Cramming several values into one column makes them impossible to count, total, or filter one at a time - which is precisely why the connecting table exists.
`ITEM` stores the catalog price, but it cannot record that invoice 50712 bought one AV07 at 64.99 - that fact belongs to the order, not the product.
Correct - invoice 50712 has many items and CF21 sits on many invoices, so `INVOICE_LINE` carries one row per (`INVOICE_NUM`, `ITEM_ID`) pairing.
questions.takeaway: A many-to-many relationship is resolved by a connecting table with one row per pairing, never by adding one more column.

questions.scenarioTitle: The invoice that changed by itself
questions.stem: Invoice 50710 sold 3 units of CF21 at 42.50 each on June 14. In July, KimTay raises CF21's catalog `PRICE` in `ITEM` to 46.00. KimTay's bookkeeper reprints invoice 50710 and it still bills 42.50 per unit. Why?
options: `INVOICE_LINE` stores `QUOTED_PRICE`, the price agreed at the time of sale, so a later `ITEM.PRICE` change cannot touch it
Once an invoice exists, the DBMS locks `ITEM.PRICE` so that item's price can never be changed again
`QUOTED_PRICE` is a foreign key pointing at `ITEM.PRICE`, and foreign keys always keep the older value
The DBMS reads `INVOICE_DATE` and automatically recalculates what the price must have been on June 14
optionNotes: Correct - `QUOTED_PRICE` is a value stored on the invoice line itself, which is why history stays accurate when the catalog price moves.
Nothing locks `ITEM.PRICE`; prices are supposed to change, and the design protects old invoices instead of freezing the catalog.
A foreign key points at another table's primary key and always shows that row's current value - it would have changed the total, not preserved it.
No database reconstructs past prices on its own; the old price survives only because someone chose to store it at sale time.
questions.takeaway: Store a value that must not move later, like `QUOTED_PRICE`, rather than looking it up from a table that keeps changing.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: the StayWell tables

questions.scenarioTitle: Room 101, twice over
questions.stem: StayWell's `ROOM` table holds room 101 at Millbrook Commons (P100) renting for 595.00 and room 101 at Sycamore Court (P200) renting for 610.00. The developer building the table first tried to make `ROOM_NUM` the primary key on its own. Why does that fail?
options: Room numbers are stored as text, and a primary key column has to hold numbers
The value 101 identifies two different rooms, so only `PROPERTY_ID` and `ROOM_NUM` together pick out one row
`ROOM` cannot have a primary key at all, because it already stores `PROPERTY_ID` as a foreign key
Sycamore Court should renumber its rooms so no room number is ever reused at another property
optionNotes: `PROPERTY_ID` is text as well and it is part of the key; a primary key value only has to be unique and always present, not numeric.
Correct - a composite primary key is used exactly when no single column is unique on its own, and (`PROPERTY_ID`, `ROOM_NUM`) is unique for every room StayWell owns.
A column can be a foreign key and part of the primary key at the same time - `ROOM.PROPERTY_ID` is both.
Renumbering real rooms to rescue a weak key changes the business to fit the table; the composite key lets each property number its own rooms freely.
questions.takeaway: When one column's values repeat across rows, combine it with another column into a composite primary key instead of forcing the business to change.

questions.scenarioTitle: The rent that should not have moved
questions.stem: Trang Nguyen signed lease L001 for room 101 at Millbrook Commons at 595.00 a month. For next year StayWell raises that room's `MONTHLY_RENT` in `ROOM` to 640.00. A new developer on the project says `LEASE.MONTHLY_RENT` is duplicated data and should be deleted. What does Lesson 1-3 say?
options: The developer is right; the column is redundant, and a lease should always read the current rent from `ROOM`
`STUDENT` should store `MONTHLY_RENT` as well, so every table involved agrees on one number
`LEASE` keeps its own `MONTHLY_RENT` on purpose, so a signed lease stays at 595.00 while `ROOM` shows 640.00 for future tenants
The DBMS will reject the `ROOM` update, because two tables would then hold different rent amounts
optionNotes: Deleting it would rewrite history - the signed lease would silently jump to 640.00 the moment the room's rate changed.
`STUDENT` describes the person, not the agreement; putting rent there is real redundancy that serves no purpose.
Correct - the lesson calls this intentional: rent can change for future tenants without rewriting a lease that was already signed.
A DBMS does not compare unrelated columns in different tables; these two numbers are allowed to differ because they mean different things.
questions.takeaway: Two columns holding the same number are not automatically redundancy - `LEASE.MONTHLY_RENT` records what was agreed, `ROOM.MONTHLY_RENT` records what is charged now.

questions.scenarioTitle: Two checks, one lease
questions.stem: Lease L001 has two `PAYMENT` rows so far: 595.00 on August 1 and 595.00 on September 1. Millbrook Commons manager Diane Ortiz asks why StayWell does not just keep one AMOUNT_PAID of 1190.00 on the `LEASE` row instead. What is the best answer?
options: Because one lease has many payments, and a single total would throw away each payment's own date and amount
Because `LEASE_ID` is `PAYMENT`'s primary key, so each lease may appear in `PAYMENT` exactly once
Because each payment belongs to a different student, and two students cannot share one lease row
Because a database cannot add numbers together, so every amount has to be listed out separately
optionNotes: Correct - the lesson calls `PAYMENT` the place where one-to-many really pays off: one lease, many monthly payments, each on its own row with its own date.
`PAYMENT_ID` is `PAYMENT`'s primary key; `LEASE_ID` is a foreign key, and it is supposed to repeat once for every payment made.
Both payments belong to lease L001 and therefore to the one student who signed it - the repetition here is across months, not across students.
Totals are easy to calculate from stored rows; the rows exist to preserve the detail that a single total would destroy.
questions.takeaway: On the many side of a one-to-many relationship, each event gets its own row so no detail is lost.

questions.scenarioTitle: Who manages Layla Ibrahim's building?
questions.stem: Layla Ibrahim is student S003 and holds lease L003. StayWell needs to know which manager to call about her building. Which chain of tables gets there, following the foreign keys stored on each table?
options: `STUDENT` to `MANAGER` directly, because `STUDENT` stores the `MANAGER_ID` of the student's building
`STUDENT` to `LEASE` to `PAYMENT` to `MANAGER`, because rent payments are collected by the manager
`STUDENT` to `LEASE` to `ROOM` to `MANAGER`, because the manager is recorded on the room the student rents
`STUDENT` to `LEASE` to `PROPERTY` to `MANAGER`, because `LEASE` stores `PROPERTY_ID` and `PROPERTY` stores `MANAGER_ID`
optionNotes: `STUDENT` holds only the student's own details - ID, name, email, home state - and has no link to a manager.
`PAYMENT` points back up to `LEASE` and stops there; it holds no property or manager information at all.
`ROOM` describes the physical room - type, rent, occupancy - and carries no `MANAGER_ID`; a manager belongs to the whole property.

Correct - `LEASE` holds `PROPERTY_ID` as a foreign key and `PROPERTY` holds `MANAGER_ID`, so the chain is `STUDENT`, `LEASE`, `PROPERTY`, `MANAGER`. The diagram routes `LEASE` through `ROOM` to `PROPERTY`, but because `LEASE` stores `PROPERTY_ID` itself, `PROPERTY` is reachable in one step.
questions.takeaway: To answer a question, follow the foreign keys table by table - each one names exactly which table it points at.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: key terms

questions.scenarioTitle: Naming what you are pointing at
questions.stem: A tutor opens StayWell's `STUDENT` table, points at the `EMAIL` column holding tnguyen@example.edu, and asks what this course calls that named column. Which answer uses the course's key terms correctly?
options: A record, because it is one specific piece of information about one specific student
A field, because `EMAIL` is one named column - the smallest named unit of data in the table
A table, because every student in the system has one email address
A database, because the value is stored in StayWell's system rather than on paper
optionNotes: A record is a whole row - the student's ID, last name, first name, email, and home state together - not one column of it.
Correct - the course defines a field, or column, as the smallest named unit of data in a table, such as `CUSTOMER_NAME` or `EMAIL`.
A table is the named collection of records that all share the same fields; `STUDENT` is the table, `EMAIL` is one of its fields.
A database is the whole structured collection of related tables - `MANAGER`, `PROPERTY`, `ROOM`, `STUDENT`, `LEASE`, and `PAYMENT` together.
questions.takeaway: Field is a column, record is a row, table is all the rows sharing those fields, and database is all the related tables.

questions.scenarioTitle: Is this redundancy or not?
questions.stem: KimTay's new bookkeeper is asked to hunt for data redundancy in the database. She notices that `CUSTOMER_NUM` 1120 appears on the `CUSTOMER` row for Access Pet Center and again on invoice 50710. Using this course's definition of data redundancy, what should she conclude?
options: It is redundancy, because a well-designed database never stores the same value in two different tables
It is redundancy, because `INVOICE` could look the customer up without storing anything at all
It is not redundancy - 1120 is a foreign key reference, and the customer's actual facts are stored only once in `CUSTOMER`
It is not redundancy, because redundancy only counts once three or more files store the same fact
optionNotes: Every foreign key by definition repeats a value that also exists in the table it points at - that shared value is the link itself. Redundancy is about repeating a fact such as a name, address, or price.
Without storing `CUSTOMER_NUM`, an invoice would have no way to say whose order it is; the key is the minimum needed to make the connection.
Correct - the name, street, and balance for Access Pet Center exist in exactly one place, which is what the definition of redundancy actually asks about.
The definition says the same fact stored in more than one place, so two copies already qualify; the count is not what makes this case different.
questions.takeaway: Repeating a key value to link tables is a reference, not redundancy; redundancy is copying the underlying facts.

matchers.heading: Sort the file-system symptoms
matchers.prompt: KimTay's office once ran on three spreadsheets and a Word file. Drop each symptom under the file-system problem it demonstrates. Each correct drop reveals why it counts as that problem.

zones.label: Data redundancy
zones.hint: One fact stored in several places, all copies still agreeing

zones.label: Data inconsistency
zones.hint: Copies exist and now give different answers

zones.label: Data isolation
zones.hint: Nothing links the files, so data cannot be combined

zones.label: Limited sharing and security
zones.hint: Who may open, change, or wait for a file

cards.text: invoices_2026.docx prints the customer's full name and address on every invoice, and customer_list.xlsx holds that same name and address once more; today every copy agrees.
cards.why: One address is written down once per invoice plus once in the customer file - one fact, many copies, which is redundancy even while they all match.

cards.text: Each rep's name is typed into rep_commissions.xlsx and typed again beside every customer in customer_list.xlsx, and all the copies currently match.
cards.why: Storing the rep's name beside every customer repeats a fact that rep_commissions.xlsx already records once.

cards.text: invoices_2026.docx spells the account 'Downtown Aquarium and Pets' while customer_list.xlsx has it as 'Downtown Aquarium & Pets'.
cards.why: Two files give two different answers about the same customer's name, and nothing says which one is right.

cards.text: invoices_2026.docx prints Whiskers & Wags Boutique in Brookville, but customer_list.xlsx still shows the boutique at its old Maple Grove address.
cards.why: One copy was updated after the move and the other was not, so the files now disagree about one fact.

cards.text: Producing one monthly sales report means retyping rep names out of one spreadsheet and order totals out of a Word file into a third document by hand.
cards.why: The answer spans files that were never designed to be combined.

cards.text: The rep spreadsheet and the invoice document share no customer code, so nothing can be matched up automatically.
cards.why: With no shared key, the files stay separate islands of data.

cards.text: The invoice file is locked while the bookkeeper has it open, so the shipping clerk has to wait.
cards.why: A file is typically used by one program or one person at a time.

cards.text: Anyone who can open customer_list.xlsx can retype a customer's address or phone number, and nothing records who changed it.
cards.why: Files offer little control over who is allowed to see or change what.

matchers.heading: One question, one table
matchers.prompt: Each business question below can be answered from a single KimTay table, with no join needed. Drop each question on the table that actually holds the answer.

zones.label: REP
zones.hint: One row per sales rep: name, city, commission, rate

zones.label: CUSTOMER
zones.hint: One row per store account: balance, credit limit, assigned rep number

zones.label: ITEM
zones.hint: One row per catalog product: category, on hand, catalog price

zones.label: INVOICE_LINE
zones.hint: One row per invoice-and-item pairing: quantity and price billed

cards.text: Which customers owe us more than $2,000 right now?
cards.why: `BALANCE` is stored directly on the customer's row, so `CUSTOMER` alone answers it.

cards.text: Which customer accounts are assigned to rep number 20?
cards.why: `CUSTOMER.REP_NUM` holds the rep's number, and only `CUSTOMER` lists accounts.

cards.text: What commission rate does rep 35 earn?
cards.why: `RATE` is a `REP` column and appears in no other table.

cards.text: Which of our sales reps work out of Brookville?
cards.why: Each rep's own `CITY` is stored on the `REP` row.

cards.text: How many Nylon Dog Leashes are on hand, and at what level do we reorder?
cards.why: `ON_HAND` and `REORDER_LEVEL` are both columns of `ITEM`.

cards.text: Which catalog products are in the Habitat category?
cards.why: `CATEGORY` describes the product itself, so it lives in `ITEM`.

cards.text: How many units of GR15 did invoice 50711 order, and what price was billed on that line?
cards.why: `NUM_ORDERED` and `QUOTED_PRICE` sit on the `INVOICE_LINE` row for that invoice-item pairing.

cards.text: Which item codes appear on invoice 50710?
cards.why: `INVOICE_LINE` has one row per item on an invoice; `INVOICE` itself lists no items.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: the four data models

questions.scenarioTitle: The room with two owners
questions.stem: StayWell's legacy filing system stores every room record underneath exactly one property, so the record for Millbrook Commons' Room 101 hangs under that one property and nowhere else. The maintenance office now needs each of those rooms to also be reachable from the crew that services it, and the old system simply cannot do it. Which data model was created as the fix for this exact two-parent problem?
options: The network model, which lets a child record have more than one parent and forms a graph instead of a tree
The hierarchical model, because a tree can simply add a second branch above any child record that needs one
The relational model, because it is the only model that stores data in rows and columns at all
The object-oriented model, because inheritance lets a Room belong to two different classes at the same time
optionNotes: Correct - the network model is the generalization of the hierarchical model in which a child record may have several parents, standardized as CODASYL.
A hierarchical database is a strict tree: every child gets exactly one parent, so there is no legal place to hang that room record a second time.
Hierarchical and network systems stored records too; what makes relational different is linking by matching key values, and it was not the historical answer to this problem.
Inheritance means one class is a kind of another class, not that a record has two owners; a Room is not a kind of maintenance crew.
questions.takeaway: Hierarchical gives every child exactly one parent; the network model was the historical fix that allowed a record to have more than one.

questions.scenarioTitle: The question nobody planned for
questions.stem: KimTay's sales manager suddenly asks something nobody anticipated: which customers of rep 20, Valerie Kaiser, have ever bought item CF21? No path for that question was built into the database when it was designed. Why can a relational database answer it without anyone redesigning the schema?
options: Because a relational database stores a pre-built pointer from every record to every other record it might ever need
Because the designer must have anticipated that exact question and built a navigation path for it in advance
Because the tables are connected by matching key values, so a new relationship can be queried with SQL after the fact
Because a relational database keeps every column in one big table, so no connection between tables is ever required
optionNotes: Stored parent-child pointers are the older hierarchical and network approach; relational tables hold no pointers, only shared key values.
Having to anticipate every access path in advance is precisely the limitation of the hierarchical and network models that the relational model removed.
Correct - a CUSTOMER row relates to a REP row simply because they share a REP_NUM value, and an INVOICE_LINE row reaches an ITEM the same way, so any relationship can be joined later.
Relational design deliberately keeps REP, CUSTOMER, INVOICE, INVOICE_LINE, and ITEM separate; cramming every column into one wide table is the redundancy problem from Lesson 1-1.
questions.takeaway: Relational tables link through matching key values, so the database can answer questions its designer never planned for.

questions.scenarioTitle: The class that borrowed its parent's fields
questions.stem: A StayWell developer sketches a Lease class that stores the lease data and also owns a monthsRemaining() method that computes an answer from that data. She then adds SubletLease, which reuses everything Lease has and adds a subtenant, and RenewalLease, which adds a priorLeaseId. Which model is she sketching, and what feature is doing the work?
options: The hierarchical model, because Lease sits above the two other boxes like a parent record over its child records
The network model, because SubletLease has two parents: the Lease class and the monthsRemaining() method
The relational model, because Lease, SubletLease, and RenewalLease would each be stored as a separate table
The object-oriented model, using inheritance so that SubletLease is a Lease with extra attributes and shared methods
optionNotes: A hierarchical tree links stored data records such as PROPERTY and ROOM; inheritance shares attributes and behavior between class definitions, which is a different idea.
A method is behavior that belongs to a class, not a second owning record; the network model is about one record having more than one parent record.
Storing the idea in tables is what you would do to keep it relationally, but a sketch with methods attached to the data is object-oriented by definition.
Correct - the object-oriented model bundles data with the behavior that acts on it, in classes that inherit from one another.
questions.takeaway: Data bundled with its behavior, in classes that inherit from other classes, is the signature of the object-oriented model.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: functional dependence

questions.scenarioTitle: The pattern that was only a coincidence
questions.stem: StayWell's four sample students are Nguyen, Carter, Ibrahim, and Park, and no two last names match. A StayWell design intern concludes that LAST_NAME pins down exactly one student, so she writes LAST_NAME -> STUDENT_ID as a functional dependency. Is she right?
options: Yes, because in the STUDENT table as it stands, no two students share a last name
No, because a dependency must hold for every row the business could ever store, and two students can share a last name
No, because only a column that has already been declared the primary key is allowed to be a determinant
No, because LAST_NAME holds text, and only numeric columns can determine other columns
optionNotes: A pattern that holds across four sample rows is a coincidence, not a business rule; the next Park who enrolls destroys it.
Correct - a true functional dependency has to hold for every possible row, which is why designers trust ZIP -> CITY, STATE but not accidental patterns in a small sample.
Any column or set of columns can be a determinant; ZIP is the lesson's example and it is not a primary key anywhere in these schemas.
Data type is irrelevant here - ITEM_ID and ZIP are both text-like, and both genuinely determine other columns.
questions.takeaway: A functional dependency is a business rule that must hold for every possible row, not a pattern that happens to hold in a small sample.

questions.scenarioTitle: Two rooms numbered 101
questions.stem: Millbrook Commons rents its Room 101 for 595.00 a month. Sycamore Court has a Room 101 of its own, and that one rents for 610.00. On her design worksheet the same intern writes ROOM_NUM -> MONTHLY_RENT. Which statement correctly captures the real dependency in the ROOM table?
options: ROOM_NUM -> MONTHLY_RENT holds, because the room number is what is painted on the door of the room
MONTHLY_RENT -> (PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM) holds, because the rent amount tells you which room you are looking at
PROPERTY_ID -> MONTHLY_RENT holds, because each property sets a single rent for the whole building
(PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM) -> MONTHLY_RENT holds, a composite determinant, because only the pair names one specific room
optionNotes: The value 101 sits on two different ROOM rows, one carrying 595.00 and one carrying 610.00, so one determinant value points at two dependent values and the definition fails.
The arrow runs from determinant to dependent, and two rooms can easily charge the same rent, so a rent amount cannot pin down one room.
Millbrook Commons alone charges 595.00 for room 101 and 450.00 for room 102, so one PROPERTY_ID value is attached to several different rents.
Correct - only the combination of which property and which room determines a single rent, which is exactly what a composite determinant means.
questions.takeaway: When one column's value repeats across genuinely different things, the determinant has to be a combination of columns.

questions.scenarioTitle: One lease, two payments
questions.stem: The same design intern moves on to PAYMENT, which stores PAYMENT_ID, LEASE_ID, PAYMENT_DATE, and AMOUNT. She claims LEASE_ID -> AMOUNT because each lease has one rent figure. Lease L001 already has two payment rows recorded against it - both of them happen to be 595.00 - and StayWell is about to start recording security deposits and partial payments in the same table. Does the dependency hold?
options: It fails, because one LEASE_ID can sit on many payment rows carrying different AMOUNT values; PAYMENT_ID is the determinant here
It holds, because LEASE_ID is a foreign key in PAYMENT, and a foreign key determines every other column in its row
It fails, because functional dependence only counts when the determinant is made of two or more columns together
It holds, because AMOUNT and LEASE.MONTHLY_RENT are both money columns that store the same kind of value
optionNotes: Correct - one LEASE_ID can sit on many payment rows, and although today's two rows for L001 both happen to be 595.00, nothing stops a deposit, a partial payment, and a full month's rent from carrying three different AMOUNT values under that same LEASE_ID, so only PAYMENT_ID determines one amount.
Being a foreign key says a value must match a row in another table; it says nothing about determining the rest of this row, and here it clearly does not.
Single-column determinants are perfectly normal - ITEM_ID -> DESCRIPTION and CUSTOMER_NUM -> CUSTOMER_NAME are both single-column dependencies.
Storing the same kind of value is not a dependency; a lease can take a deposit, a partial payment, and a catch-up payment, all different amounts.
questions.takeaway: A -> B only holds when one value of A never sits beside two different values of B - and it has to be impossible, not merely absent from today's rows.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: primary keys

questions.scenarioTitle: The invoice with no number
questions.stem: A KimTay clerk saves a new invoice for Access Pet Center but leaves INVOICE_NUM blank, planning to type the number in later when the paper form comes back from the warehouse. In the spreadsheet she used before, a blank cell was harmless. In a DBMS that enforces entity integrity, which rule does the blank primary key break?
options: Nothing is broken, because a NULL simply means the value is unknown for now and can be filled in later
It breaks the composite key rule, because INVOICE_NUM must always be paired with ITEM_ID to count as valid
It breaks entity integrity: a primary key value may never be missing, so nothing can identify or reference that invoice
It is allowed as long as no other invoice row is blank too, since two blanks would be duplicate key values
optionNotes: A NULL in an ordinary column is fine - STUDENT.EMAIL is declared `EMAIL VARCHAR(30)` with no NOT NULL, so it may legally be empty - but a NULL primary key leaves a row that no query and no INVOICE_LINE row can ever point to.
The composite key (INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID) belongs to INVOICE_LINE; the INVOICE table is identified by INVOICE_NUM alone.
Correct - entity integrity means the primary key is unique and never missing for every row in the table.
Entity integrity has two halves, no duplicates and no missing values, so a single blank key breaks it even if it is the only one.
questions.takeaway: Entity integrity means every primary key value is present and unique - a blank key value is never acceptable.

questions.scenarioTitle: The email column nobody constrained
questions.stem: STUDENT stores STUDENT_ID and EMAIL, and the shipped schema declares `EMAIL VARCHAR(30)` with no NOT NULL and no UNIQUE constraint. All four students on file happen to have an address and no two of them match, and LEASE rows point at students using STUDENT_ID. Layla Ibrahim then replaces her personal address with a new university one. Which column should be STUDENT's primary key, and what is EMAIL's real status?
options: EMAIL should be the primary key, because all four students on file have one and no two of them match
EMAIL is a candidate key that merely lost the contest, so it is STUDENT's alternate key
STUDENT_ID and EMAIL should be combined into a composite primary key so that a change of address is recorded
STUDENT_ID, because it is guaranteed unique and present, never changes, and is what LEASE already references - while EMAIL as declared is guaranteed neither
optionNotes: Four tidy sample rows are a coincidence, not a guarantee - the same sample fallacy as LAST_NAME -> STUDENT_ID, and here the schema itself would accept a duplicate address or none at all.

A candidate key must be unique and never null for every possible row; because EMAIL is declared without NOT NULL or UNIQUE, the DBMS would happily store a second student with Layla's old address, so EMAIL is not a candidate key and cannot be an alternate key here.
Composite keys are for tables where no single column identifies a row; STUDENT_ID already does, and pairing them would make the key change every time an email does and let a NULL into the key.
Correct - STUDENT_ID is stable, always present, unique, and already referenced by LEASE, while EMAIL carries no uniqueness or not-null guarantee at all.
questions.takeaway: A column is only a candidate key when the schema guarantees it is unique and never missing; and among real candidates, choose the one that never changes.

questions.scenarioTitle: Two payments on the same day
questions.stem: A StayWell design intern sketches a redesign of PAYMENT and proposes that the pair (LEASE_ID, PAYMENT_DATE) serve as the primary key instead of PAYMENT_ID, reasoning that a lease normally receives one payment a month. Bruce Feldman confirms that most of his tenants do pay once a month, and the four payment rows on file do happen to have distinct lease-and-date pairs. Apply the same repeat-across-different-things test the lesson uses when deciding whether a column needs a partner. What is wrong with her plan?
options: Nothing is wrong, because a composite key built from two columns is always safer than relying on a single column
The pair fails the test: a deposit and a first rent payment recorded on the same day are different rows that would collide
The pair fails because a primary key is never allowed to include a date column under any circumstances
The pair fails because LEASE_ID is a foreign key, and a foreign key can never be part of a primary key
optionNotes: More columns does not mean more unique; a composite key is only correct when no single column identifies a row, and PAYMENT_ID already does that on its own.

Correct - the test asks whether the value could repeat across rows that are genuinely different things, and two payments posted to one lease on one date do exactly that, no matter how tidy today's four rows look.
Dates are legal inside keys - the trouble is repetition, not the data type, and the same pair would be just as unsafe built from any other repeatable column.
ROOM's primary key is (PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM), and PROPERTY_ID is also a foreign key to PROPERTY, so a foreign key can absolutely sit inside a primary key.
questions.takeaway: Add a column to the key only when no single column identifies a row, then run the repeat test on the combination itself.

matchers.heading: Match the database to its data model
matchers.prompt: Click a card, then click the model it describes. Each card belongs to exactly one of the four models from Lesson 2-1.

cards.text: ROOM records hang as a branch under PROPERTY in a strict tree, and the only way to reach a room is to walk down from its one parent record.
cards.why: A strict tree gives every child record exactly one parent and exactly one path to it.

cards.text: IBM's IMS, the classic historical example, required you to enter through the parent record to reach anything beneath it.
cards.why: IMS is the system built on the strict-tree model, where one parent owns the only route in.

cards.text: To reach a record you followed a stored access path down from an owner record, and a single record was allowed to sit under more than one owner at once.
cards.why: Allowing a record several owners turns the tree into a graph, which is this model's defining move.

cards.text: Standardized as CODASYL in the 1970s; the stored links formed a graph rather than a tree.
cards.why: CODASYL is the name for the standardized version of the graph-shaped model.

cards.text: An INVOICE row is tied to a CUSTOMER row only because both of them store the same CUSTOMER_NUM value.
cards.why: Tables connect through matching key values, not stored parent-child pointers.

cards.text: MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, and Access all run on it, and so does this entire course.
cards.why: Every mainstream system in the lesson's comparison table is relational.

cards.text: Each stored object carries both its data and the code that operates on it, so the rent calculation travels with the lease itself.
cards.why: Bundling data together with the behavior that acts on it in one stored object is the object-oriented signature.

cards.text: Chosen for CAD drawings and multimedia systems, where a stored item is a complex object rather than a row of simple values.
cards.why: Complex objects with their own behavior are what put CAD and multimedia in this model's niche.

matchers.heading: Sort the columns: could this be a primary key?
matchers.prompt: Click a column card, then click the zone that fits it. Exactly one zone is defensible per card: ask whether the value repeats, whether the business can change it after it is assigned, and whether pairing it with one specific partner column is what makes this table's declared key.

zones.label: Good primary key
zones.hint: Unique on its own, never missing, never edited after it is assigned

zones.label: Descriptive only
zones.hint: The value already repeats across rows, and pairing it with another column still would not make it this table's key

zones.label: Unique but volatile
zones.hint: Distinct on every row today, but the business can change the value later

zones.label: Needs a composite key
zones.hint: Not unique alone, but IS this table's declared key once paired with one specific partner column

cards.text: REP.REP_NUM - assigned once by KimTay, never blank, never reused, never edited.
cards.why: Unique, always present, and stable is exactly what a primary key needs to be.

cards.text: LEASE.LEASE_ID - one value assigned when a lease is signed, and it stays with that lease until the row is gone.
cards.why: It identifies one lease row on its own and never changes, so PAYMENT rows can safely reference it.

cards.text: ITEM.CATEGORY - AV07 and FT88 both carry the value Habitat, so the value cannot name one product, and no partner column would turn it into the key because ITEM_ID already is.
cards.why: A value shared by several rows can never identify one row, and it is not half of this table's declared key either.

cards.text: CUSTOMER.CITY - Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic are both in Maple Grove, so one value already names two different customers, and no partner column would make CITY part of CUSTOMER's key because CUSTOMER_NUM already is.
cards.why: The value provably repeats in the shipped rows, and it is not half of CUSTOMER's declared key.

cards.text: PROPERTY.PROPERTY_NAME - no two StayWell buildings share a name, but Millbrook Commons is about to be rebranded.
cards.why: A name is distinct today, but renaming it would force every row that referenced it to be rewritten.

cards.text: MANAGER.PHONE - Diane Ortiz and Bruce Feldman list different numbers, but Bruce is about to change his.
cards.why: Distinct today is not enough; a primary key value has to stay put.

cards.text: ROOM.ROOM_NUM - the value 101 appears under two different properties, but it is half of ROOM's declared primary key, `PRIMARY KEY (PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM)`.
cards.why: Alone it repeats across buildings; paired with its one partner column it names exactly one room.

cards.text: INVOICE_LINE.ITEM_ID - CF21 sits on invoice 50710 and on invoice 50711, but paired with INVOICE_NUM it is the declared primary key of INVOICE_LINE.
cards.why: Alone it repeats across invoices; paired with INVOICE_NUM it identifies exactly one invoice line.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: the five design phases

questions.scenarioTitle: The requirements nobody gathered
questions.stem: KimTay's owner emails a developer a list of column names and says "just build this table by Friday." Nobody has looked at the invoices, stock sheets, or reports the bookkeeper and the warehouse staff actually work from today. According to this course's five design phases, what should happen before anything else?
options: Pick the DBMS and the data type for every column, then show the owner the result
Gather requirements: establish what questions the database must answer and what data already exists
Create the tables now and normalize them later, once real data exposes the problems
Draw the ER diagram straight from the owner's column list and treat that list as the requirements
optionNotes: Data types and DBMS choice are physical design, phase four, and cannot be decided sensibly before anyone knows what the system must do.
Requirements gathering is phase one -- you work out what questions the database must answer and what data the business already keeps, before designing anything.
Building first skips phases one through three entirely, and there is nothing to normalize until requirements and a conceptual design exist.
A list of column names is one person's guess; conceptual design needs the real business questions behind it, which the existing paperwork reveals.
questions.takeaway: Design starts with people, not columns: gather requirements before anything is drawn or built.

questions.scenarioTitle: Picking VARCHAR and an index
questions.stem: StayWell's ER diagram is finished and the tables have been normalized on paper. The developer now decides ROOM_TYPE will be `VARCHAR(10)`, adds an index on STUDENT.LAST_NAME, and chooses MySQL as the DBMS. Which design phase is the developer working in?
options: Requirements gathering, because index choices come from what the users said they needed
Conceptual design, because the developer is still deciding what the database will store
Logical design, because choosing a column's type is part of choosing its key
Physical design, because data types, constraints, indexes, and DBMS choice are physical decisions
optionNotes: Requirements gathering collects business questions, not column types, and it happens long before any DBMS is chosen.
Conceptual design ends once the entities, attributes, and relationships are settled, and the ER diagram here is already done.
Logical design turns the diagram into tables with primary and foreign keys; the type stored in a column is a separate, later decision.
Concrete data types, constraints, indexes, and which DBMS to implement in are exactly what phase four, physical design, covers.
questions.takeaway: Data types, indexes, constraints, and DBMS choice all belong to physical design, phase four.

questions.scenarioTitle: Normalizing after go-live
questions.stem: A developer drafting KimTay's database built a flat INVOICE table that repeats the customer's city on every invoice row, then loaded 4,000 rows into it. Noticing the repetition only now, the developer says it can be "normalized later, since the DBMS will sort it out." What is wrong with that plan?
options: Nothing is wrong, because normalization is part of physical design and is meant to happen after loading data
Nothing is wrong, because the DBMS collapses the repeated city values on its own once an index is added
Normalization belongs to logical design, before implementation, so fixing it now means migrating live data
Normalization should have happened during requirements gathering, before anyone talked to the users
optionNotes: Physical design covers data types, constraints, and indexes; normalization is a logical-design step that comes before any of that.
An index speeds up lookups, but it never removes redundant repeated values or the update anomalies they cause.
Normalization is phase three, logical design, so doing it after 4,000 rows are loaded turns a paper decision into a risky data migration.
Requirements gathering is phase one and produces business questions, not tables, so there is nothing to normalize until logical design creates them.
questions.takeaway: Normalize during logical design, on paper -- after go-live it becomes a data migration.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF

questions.scenarioTitle: Three rooms in one cell
questions.stem: A flat StayWell property report gives Sycamore Court (P200) one row whose ROOM_NUMS cell reads "101, 201, 202", while Millbrook Commons' row reads "101, 102". Which normalization rule does this break, and what is the fix?
options: 2NF, because ROOM_NUMS depends on only part of the report's composite key, so it moves to a ROOM table
3NF, because the room numbers depend on the manager's name, so MANAGER moves into its own table
1NF, because the cell holds a list instead of one atomic value, so each room gets its own row
Nothing, because the column is wide enough to hold the whole list and the report still prints
optionNotes: A partial dependency is a 2NF problem about composite keys, and it never explains three values crammed into one cell -- 1NF has to be satisfied first.
A transitive dependency is a 3NF problem where one non-key column drives another, and room numbers are not determined by the manager's name.
1NF requires every column to hold a single atomic value, so the repeating group becomes one ROOM row per room: P200/101, P200/201, and P200/202.
It fits in the column, but a list is not one value: you cannot count rooms, join to LEASE, or price one room, which is precisely why 1NF exists.
questions.takeaway: 1NF first: no cell may hold a list, so every repeating group becomes its own rows.

questions.scenarioTitle: The description that rides along
questions.stem: A KimTay table has the composite key (INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID) and also stores DESCRIPTION. Every row that contains CF21 repeats "Grain-Free Dry Food 30lb" -- once for invoice 50710 and again for invoice 50711. What is the precise problem?
options: A partial dependency: DESCRIPTION depends on ITEM_ID alone, which is only part of the key
A transitive dependency: DESCRIPTION depends on another non-key column in the same table
A repeating group: the same text value shows up on more than one row of the table
No problem at all: DESCRIPTION is not part of the primary key, so it may hold any value
optionNotes: 2NF demands that every non-key column depend on the whole key, and DESCRIPTION needs only ITEM_ID, so it belongs in ITEM.
Transitive means a non-key column drives another non-key column; here the determinant, ITEM_ID, is part of the primary key, which makes it partial instead.
A repeating group is several values inside one cell, which is a different symptom from a value legitimately repeating down a column.
Sitting outside the key is not permission to sit anywhere: a non-key column must depend on the entire key or move to another table.
questions.takeaway: If a non-key column needs only part of a composite key, that is a partial dependency and 2NF moves it out.

questions.scenarioTitle: Valerie Kaiser changes her name
questions.stem: KimTay keeps one table keyed by CUSTOMER_NUM that also stores CUSTOMER_NAME, REP_NUM, and REP_LAST_NAME. Rep 20, Valerie Kaiser, serves both Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic, so when she changes her last name a clerk has to edit it on every one of her customer rows -- and one row gets missed. What is the underlying design flaw?
options: The table is not in 1NF, because the rep's last name appears on more than one row
The table is not in 2NF, because REP_LAST_NAME depends on only part of a composite key
The table is not in 3NF, and the fix is to drop REP_NUM and keep REP_LAST_NAME
The table is not in 3NF: REP_LAST_NAME depends on REP_NUM, a non-key column, not on CUSTOMER_NUM
optionNotes: 1NF is about lists inside a single cell; a value repeating down a column is what 2NF and 3NF address.
CUSTOMER_NUM is a single-column key, so there is no part of it for anything to depend on: a table whose primary key is one column cannot have a partial dependency and is automatically in 2NF.
The normal form is right but the fix is backwards -- dropping REP_NUM destroys the link to the rep, while 3NF removes the descriptive column and keeps the foreign key.
That is a transitive dependency, CUSTOMER_NUM to REP_NUM to REP_LAST_NAME, and moving rep details into REP stores the name in one place.
questions.takeaway: When a non-key column determines another non-key column, split the determinant into its own table and keep the foreign key.

questions.scenarioTitle: The building with no tenants yet
questions.stem: StayWell is taking over a third building, Cedar Ridge, and no student has signed a lease there yet. In the old flat lease report, where every row has to start with a student, there is nowhere to record that Cedar Ridge exists at all. Which anomaly is this?
options: A deletion anomaly, because removing the last student would erase the building from the records
An insertion anomaly, because a new property cannot be recorded until some student leases there
An update anomaly, because the building's name would have to be corrected on many rows at once
A partial dependency, because the building's details depend on only part of the table's key
optionNotes: A deletion anomaly is losing a fact when you remove a row, but nothing is being removed here -- the fact cannot get in at all.
That is the insertion anomaly exactly, and a separate PROPERTY table lets Cedar Ridge exist with zero leases attached.
An update anomaly is one fact stored in many rows drifting out of sync; the problem here is that the fact cannot be stored even once.
A partial dependency is a structural 2NF defect, not an anomaly; anomalies are the symptoms users actually feel.
questions.takeaway: Insertion anomaly means a fact you cannot record, deletion means a fact you lose, update means a fact stored in too many places.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: reading an ER diagram

questions.scenarioTitle: A line read from the bottom up
questions.stem: On StayWell's diagram the STUDENT box is drawn below LEASE, and the vertical line between them carries two short tick marks -- this course's "exactly one" marking -- at the STUDENT end and a crow's foot at the LEASE end. What business rule does that line state?
options: One lease may name many students, and each student holds exactly one lease
Each student holds exactly one lease, and each lease names exactly one student
STUDENT and LEASE must always hold the same number of rows, matched one for one
Each lease belongs to exactly one student, and one student may hold many leases
optionNotes: That reads the line backwards: the crow's foot sits at the LEASE end, so the many-ness belongs to leases, not students.
That would require the two-tick marking at both ends; a crow's foot at the LEASE end deliberately allows a student more than one lease.
A relationship line constrains how rows match up, not how many rows each table holds; today's four students and four leases are a coincidence, not a rule.
Read each end on its own: two ticks at the STUDENT end mean exactly one student per lease, and the crow's foot at the LEASE end lets that student hold many leases.
questions.takeaway: A vertical line is read exactly like a horizontal one: the marking touching a box tells you how many of that box's rows take part.

questions.scenarioTitle: Reading one line out loud
questions.stem: On the KimTay diagram, the line joining REP and CUSTOMER carries two short tick marks -- this course's "exactly one" marking -- at the REP end and a crow's foot at the CUSTOMER end. KimTay's bookkeeper asks what business rule that encodes. What do you tell her?
options: One customer may be served by many reps, and each rep handles exactly one customer
Every rep must serve exactly one customer, and no rep is allowed a second one
One rep serves many customers, and each customer is assigned to exactly one rep
REP and CUSTOMER hold the same primary key values, matched row for row
optionNotes: This reverses the symbols -- the crow's foot sits at the CUSTOMER end, so the many-ness belongs to customers, not reps.
The two ticks sit at the REP end and fix how many reps a customer gets; the crow's foot still lets rep 20 serve both Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic.
Read each end separately: the two ticks mean exactly one on the REP side, and the crow's foot means many on the CUSTOMER side.
A relationship line means a foreign key match, not identical key values, and CUSTOMER_NUM and REP_NUM are different things entirely.
questions.takeaway: Read each end of the line on its own: the symbol nearest a box describes how many of that box's rows take part.

questions.scenarioTitle: The lamp nobody has ordered yet
questions.stem: KimTay's buyer wants to stock a turtle basking lamp that may sit unsold for months before it starts selling steadily, so KimTay asks for a diagram that plainly permits an item with no invoice lines at all. On the ITEM-INVOICE_LINE line, the INVOICE_LINE end is the end that counts how many invoice lines one item can appear on. Which marking states that relaxed rule?
options: A crow's foot with a circle, meaning zero or many invoice lines for that item
Two short tick marks, meaning each item appears on exactly one invoice line
A crow's foot with a tick, meaning one or many invoice lines with at least one required
A circle with one tick mark, meaning each item appears on at most one invoice line
optionNotes: The circle allows zero and the crow's foot allows many, which is exactly the rule for brand-new stock that may later sell often.
Two ticks mean exactly one, which would forbid unsold stock and would also forbid CF21, which already sells on invoices 50710 and 50711.
That is the stricter marking, and it is the very requirement the buyer is asking to relax: it demands that every item appear on at least one invoice line.
A circle with one tick allows zero but caps the item at a single line, and CF21 already appears on two invoice lines.
questions.takeaway: A circle allows zero and a crow's foot allows many, so together they mean optional and unlimited.

questions.scenarioTitle: The same column name in two boxes
questions.stem: A new KimTay intern spots REP_NUM twice on the ER diagram: bold and underlined at the top of the REP box, and in orange italics on the last line of the CUSTOMER box. What does the italic copy tell her?
options: Italics mark an optional attribute, so a customer is allowed to have no rep at all
Italics mark a foreign key: CUSTOMER.REP_NUM stores a value belonging to REP's primary key
Italics mark a second primary key, so CUSTOMER has two different ways to identify a row
Italics mark a calculated column that the DBMS fills in from REP each time you query
optionNotes: Optionality is shown by a circle on the relationship line, never by how an attribute name is styled.
In every diagram this course uses, orange italic text means foreign key -- a column that references another table's primary key.
A table has exactly one primary key, and this diagram shows CUSTOMER's in bold underline as CUSTOMER_NUM at the top of the box.
Nothing is computed here; REP_NUM is a stored value that must match an existing row in REP.
questions.takeaway: Bold underline means primary key and italics mean foreign key, so one column name can be both in different boxes.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: key terms in practice

questions.scenarioTitle: The email that looks like a key
questions.stem: In StayWell's STUDENT table, Layla Ibrahim's row holds STUDENT_ID S003 and an EMAIL value, and the four students on file today all have different emails. EMAIL is declared `VARCHAR(30)` with no NOT NULL rule, and StayWell does not require an applicant to supply an email or forbid two students from sharing one. Using this course's vocabulary, what is EMAIL?
options: Not a candidate key, because nothing guarantees every student has an email or that two students cannot share one
A candidate key, because the four emails on file today are all different from one another
A foreign key, because it can be used to look up which student a row belongs to
A composite key, because an email address joins a user name and a domain into one value
optionNotes: A candidate key must be guaranteed unique and never blank for every possible row, and EMAIL is guaranteed neither, so today's tidy values are a coincidence rather than a key.
Four rows that happen not to collide prove nothing about the fifth student, who may leave the column blank or share a family address.
A foreign key stores a value belonging to another table's primary key, but EMAIL belongs to STUDENT itself and points at nothing.
Composite means two or more columns acting together as one key, not two parts inside a single text value.
questions.takeaway: A candidate key is a guarantee that a value is unique and never blank for every possible row, not a pattern you happen to notice in today's data.

questions.scenarioTitle: The room 101 that would be rejected
questions.stem: Sycamore Court (P200) has a room 101, and Millbrook Commons (P100) already had one. Suppose StayWell had built ROOM with ROOM_NUM alone as the primary key instead of (PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM). On a DBMS that enforces primary keys, what happens when the leasing office inserts the Sycamore Court row?
options: It accepts the row and keeps both, since a room number only has to be unique inside its own building
It accepts the row and overwrites Millbrook Commons' room 101 with the new values
It rejects the row, because 101 is already in use as a primary key value
It rejects the row and deletes Millbrook Commons' room 101 as well, because the key collided
optionNotes: That is exactly what the real key (PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM) buys you, but with ROOM_NUM alone the DBMS has no way to tell the two rooms apart.
A primary key never silently overwrites an existing row; a colliding insert is refused and the older row is left untouched.
A primary key is a uniqueness rule the DBMS enforces, so a second row numbered 101 cannot be stored until PROPERTY_ID joins the key.
Rejecting the new row is right, but a refused insert changes nothing that is already stored -- Millbrook Commons' room 101 survives untouched.
questions.takeaway: A primary key is a uniqueness promise the DBMS enforces, so when one column's values can repeat across genuinely different rows, the key needs a second column.

questions.scenarioTitle: Why the lease carries two columns
questions.stem: StayWell's LEASE rows record the rented room as a pair of values -- L001 stores P100 and 101, while L003 stores P200 and 201. A developer asks why LEASE cannot just store ROOM_NUM and be done with it. What is the reason?
options: Because the ER diagram draws a line straight from LEASE to PROPERTY, so PROPERTY_ID has to be repeated there
Because ROOM_NUM is stored as a number while PROPERTY_ID is text, so both are needed to sort the leases
Because a foreign key must repeat every column of the table it points at, not just that table's key
Because ROOM's primary key is (PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM), and a foreign key must carry every column of the key it references
optionNotes: No line is drawn between LEASE and PROPERTY at all -- a lease reaches its property through ROOM, which is why both room columns travel together.
How a value is stored is beside the point: room 101 is ambiguous in any data type, because both buildings number a room 101.
A foreign key repeats only the referenced table's primary key columns; ROOM_TYPE, MONTHLY_RENT, and MAX_OCCUPANTS stay in ROOM.
Room 101 exists at both P100 and P200, so only the pair identifies one room, and the referencing table has to carry the pair.
questions.takeaway: When the table you point at has a composite primary key, the foreign key must carry every one of that key's columns.

matchers.heading: Which normal form does each table break?
matchers.prompt: Each card lists every column its table holds -- assume nothing else is stored. Click a card, then click the first normal form that table fails, or "Already in 3NF" if there is nothing left to fix.

cards.text: A flat invoice sheet where invoice 50710 stores ITEMS_ORDERED as "CF21, DG04" in one cell
cards.why: Two values crammed into one cell is a repeating group, the defect 1NF removes.

cards.text: A flat rep sheet storing CUSTOMERS_SERVED as "Access Pet Center, Companion Care Clinic" in one cell
cards.why: Each customer served belongs on its own row before any other normal form can be checked.

cards.text: A table holding only the key (INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID), NUM_ORDERED, and INVOICE_DATE, which depends on INVOICE_NUM alone
cards.why: INVOICE_DATE describes the whole invoice, not one line, so it hangs off only part of the key.

cards.text: A table holding only the key (STUDENT_ID, PAYMENT_DATE), AMOUNT, and HOME_STATE, which depends on STUDENT_ID alone
cards.why: HOME_STATE needs only half of the key -- the textbook partial dependency.

cards.text: A lease table holding only LEASE_ID (key), STUDENT_ID, STUDENT_LAST_NAME, and STUDENT_EMAIL
cards.why: The student's name and email depend on STUDENT_ID, a non-key column, not on LEASE_ID.

cards.text: An invoice table holding only INVOICE_NUM (key), CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, and CUSTOMER_CITY
cards.why: Customer details hang off CUSTOMER_NUM, not off the invoice number.

cards.text: A rep table holding only REP_NUM (key), LAST_NAME, FIRST_NAME, and COMMISSION
cards.why: Every listed column describes that one rep and depends on REP_NUM alone, with no city or ZIP in the table to drive anything else.

cards.text: An invoice-line table holding only the key (INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID), NUM_ORDERED, and QUOTED_PRICE
cards.why: Both remaining columns need the whole key -- the quantity and price belong to that item on that invoice.

matchers.heading: Match each ERD marking to what it tells you
matchers.prompt: Every marking on the KimTay and StayWell diagrams carries one precise meaning. Click a card, then click the zone that says what it means.

zones.label: It means many on this side

cards.text: A rectangle with a dark header bar labeled INVOICE_LINE
cards.why: Every rectangle on an ERD is an entity, and each entity becomes one table.

cards.text: A rectangle with a dark header bar labeled MANAGER
cards.why: StayWell's MANAGER box is an entity, and it became the MANAGER table.

cards.text: ITEM_ID printed bold with a line under it, on the top line of the ITEM box
cards.why: Bold plus underline is this course's notation for the primary key attribute.

cards.text: PAYMENT_ID printed bold with a line under it, on the top line of the PAYMENT box
cards.why: It is the one column chosen to identify each payment row uniquely.

cards.text: CUSTOMER_NUM printed in orange italics on the middle line of the INVOICE box, between INVOICE_NUM and INVOICE_DATE
cards.why: Orange italics mean the value must match the primary key of a row in CUSTOMER.

cards.text: LEASE_ID printed in orange italics in the PAYMENT box, just under PAYMENT_ID
cards.why: Each payment points back at the lease it is paying for.
