quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: running SQL commands

questions.scenarioTitle: KimTay's two Monday commands
questions.stem: A developer at KimTay is rebuilding the company's database from scratch, and she warms up on a cut-down two-column practice table. First she runs `CREATE TABLE REP_PRACTICE (REP_NUM CHAR(2) PRIMARY KEY, LAST_NAME VARCHAR(15) NOT NULL);` and then she runs `INSERT INTO REP_PRACTICE VALUES ('20', 'Kaiser');`. A teammate asks which SQL family each command belongs to. What is the correct answer?
options: Both are DDL, because both commands change what is stored in the practice table
CREATE TABLE is DDL because it defines structure, and INSERT is DML because it adds data
Both are DML, because she is manipulating the database in both of the two statements
CREATE TABLE is DML because it creates something, and INSERT is DDL because it defines a row
optionNotes: DDL is the family that defines structure, and INSERT defines nothing; it puts one row of data inside a structure that already exists.
Right: CREATE TABLE defines the shape of the practice table, and INSERT moves data into that shape.
DML is SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, and CREATE TABLE never touches a single row of data.
The two labels are swapped, because the 'define' in DDL means defining structure, not filling in one row.
questions.takeaway: DDL defines structure, as CREATE TABLE does; DML works with data through SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE.

questions.scenarioTitle: KimTay's week in four tasks
questions.stem: KimTay's bookkeeper lists everything she did with the database this week: she looked up Access Pet Center's balance, added a brand-new customer, fixed a typo in a customer's street, and removed an account that closed. Her manager asks which SQL commands those four tasks correspond to, in that same order. What is the right list?
options: CREATE, READ, UPDATE and DELETE, since those are the keywords you actually type in SQL
INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE, matching the order the four operations are usually taught in
SELECT and INSERT for the first two tasks, then UPDATE for both of the last two
SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, the four DML commands that make up CRUD
optionNotes: CRUD is a nickname for the four operations, not SQL syntax, so typing READ where SELECT belongs is an error.
These are the right four commands in the wrong order, because looking up a balance came first and that task is SELECT.
Removing a closed account takes the whole row out of the table, which is DELETE rather than a second UPDATE.
Correct: read is SELECT, create is INSERT, update is UPDATE and delete is DELETE, the four DML commands.
questions.takeaway: CRUD names the four jobs; SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE are the SQL commands that carry them out.

questions.scenarioTitle: The table that disappeared overnight
questions.stem: A classmate types a short table-creating statement of her own into the sandbox on this page, runs it, and gets a success message. The next morning she opens the same page and runs `SELECT * FROM PRACTICE;`, and the sandbox reports that no such table exists. Why is her table gone?
options: The statement never really ran, because SQLite requires a CREATE DATABASE statement first
Her table was saved on the course server, so she needs to sign in again before it will appear
Each sandbox is its own SQLite database held in memory, so reloading the page starts it over
Running a SELECT clears out any table you created earlier in that same sandbox session
optionNotes: SQLite has no CREATE DATABASE statement at all, and every page load already hands you a working database.
Nothing you type into a sandbox is stored on a server, so signing in would not bring the table back.
Correct: the sandbox is a SQLite database that lives only in memory, so it starts empty again on each page load.
SELECT only reads data and never removes a table; running it a hundred times would change nothing.
questions.takeaway: Each sandbox is an in-memory SQLite database that resets on page load, so keep your SQL in a saved script.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: creating a database

questions.scenarioTitle: Hunting for CREATE DATABASE in Access
questions.stem: KimTay's office manager has been told to build the company's database in Microsoft Access. He has spent twenty minutes hunting for somewhere to type `CREATE DATABASE kimtay_pet_supplies;` and cannot find it anywhere in the program. What should you tell him?
options: Access has no CREATE DATABASE statement at all, so he makes a blank .accdb file through File, New
He should type `CREATE DB kimtay;` instead, because Access abbreviates the statement to save typing
He must run CREATE DATABASE in MySQL first, and Access will then see the new database on that server
Access supports it, but only after `USE kimtay_pet_supplies;` has selected the database for him
optionNotes: Correct: in Access the database is one .accdb file, created through File, New, Blank Database.
There is no CREATE DB command in Access or in any other engine, so a shorter spelling will not help.
MySQL and Access are separate programs with separate storage, so a MySQL database is invisible to Access.
USE is a MySQL statement for switching between databases on a server, and Access has no such server.
questions.takeaway: Access has no CREATE DATABASE statement; the database is a single .accdb file created through the interface.

questions.scenarioTitle: MySQL says no database selected
questions.stem: The developer setting up KimTay's MySQL server opens MySQL Workbench on a brand-new server and immediately runs the `CREATE TABLE REP (...);` statement. MySQL refuses it with the message 'No database selected'. Which fix matches the two-step pattern this lesson shows for MySQL?
options: Prefix every column with the database name, as in `kimtay_pet_supplies.REP_NUM CHAR(2)`, on each line
Rename the table to kimtay_pet_supplies so that MySQL can work out which database it belongs to
Run `CREATE DATABASE kimtay_pet_supplies;` then `USE kimtay_pet_supplies;` before the CREATE TABLE
Nothing needs fixing, because MySQL builds a database automatically the first time you create a table
optionNotes: Column definitions never carry a database name; the database is chosen once with USE, not repeated on every column.
A table and a database are different things, so renaming the table tells MySQL nothing about where to store it.
Correct: MySQL wants the database created and then selected with USE before any table is built inside it.
MySQL never invents a database for you, which is exactly why it answered 'No database selected'.
questions.takeaway: In MySQL, CREATE DATABASE and then USE come before any CREATE TABLE statement.

questions.scenarioTitle: The Oracle login with no database name
questions.stem: KimTay's contractor sets up an Oracle version of the database and hands the company's new analyst a username and password instead of a database name. The analyst wants to know why nobody ran a `CREATE DATABASE` statement the way they would in MySQL. What is the best explanation?
options: Oracle's CREATE DATABASE works just like MySQL's, and any user with a login is allowed to run it
In Oracle a database is a whole instance a DBA builds, so day to day you work inside your own schema
Oracle keeps each database in a single file you create from a File menu, exactly the way Access does
Oracle has no notion of a database at all, so every one of its tables floats in one shared space
optionNotes: Creating an Oracle database means building an entire instance with a DBA tool, not something an ordinary user runs.
Correct: Oracle hands you a schema or user account that behaves like your own personal database.
The single-file design belongs to Microsoft Access; Oracle stores everything inside a server instance.
Oracle definitely has databases, and it separates each user's tables into that user's own schema.
questions.takeaway: In Oracle, everyday work happens inside your own schema or user account, not a database you create yourself.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: CREATE TABLE

questions.scenarioTitle: The STUDENT table that will not build
questions.stem: The developer building StayWell's STUDENT table runs `CREATE TABLE STUDENT (STUDENT_ID CHAR(4) PRIMARY KEY, LAST_NAME VARCHAR(15) NOT NULL, FIRST_NAME VARCHAR(15) NOT NULL,);` and the engine reports a syntax error near the closing parenthesis. Every column name and type is spelled correctly. Which correction fixes it?
options: Change `CHAR(4)` to `CHAR 4`, since parentheses belong only around the whole list of columns
Add VALUES before the opening parenthesis, as in `CREATE TABLE STUDENT VALUES (...)`, to name the columns
Delete the trailing comma after `FIRST_NAME VARCHAR(15) NOT NULL` so nothing follows the last column
Wrap every column name in single quotes, as in `'LAST_NAME' VARCHAR(15) NOT NULL`, all through the list
optionNotes: The size in CHAR(4) always sits in parentheses, so removing them would create a brand-new error.
VALUES belongs to INSERT, which adds rows; CREATE TABLE lists column names, types and constraints instead.
Correct: commas separate columns, so a comma with no column after it leaves the list unfinished.
In standard SQL single quotes mark text values, and an identifier is quoted with double quotes or backticks when it is quoted at all; either spelling still leaves a comma with no column after it.
questions.takeaway: Inside CREATE TABLE, commas separate columns, so the last column must not be followed by one.

questions.scenarioTitle: The email that cannot be the key
questions.stem: The developer building StayWell's STUDENT table has to choose a primary key. A teammate notices that all four students already on file have an email address and that no two addresses match, and suggests using EMAIL as the primary key instead of STUDENT_ID. What should the developer say?
options: EMAIL is a safe key here, because the four addresses already on file are all different from each other
STUDENT_ID, because the schema never requires EMAIL to be filled in, so it cannot identify every row
STUDENT_ID, but only because the primary key always has to be the first column listed in the table
Neither column can serve, because a primary key must be a number and both of these columns hold text
optionNotes: Four rows that happen to differ today guarantee nothing about tomorrow's rows, and the schema puts no uniqueness rule on EMAIL.
Correct: EMAIL is declared VARCHAR(30) with no NOT NULL, so a student row may carry no address at all, while STUDENT_ID is always there.
Column order carries no meaning in SQL, and STUDENT_ID would still be the right key if it were listed last.
Primary keys hold text all through this course, including CHAR(4) keys such as STUDENT_ID and CHAR(2) keys such as REP_NUM.
questions.takeaway: A primary key has to be present and unique on every row by the schema's own rules, which is why STUDENT_ID is the key and EMAIL is not.

questions.scenarioTitle: Two guarantees built into the table
questions.stem: KimTay wants two guarantees built into the REP table itself: no rep row can ever be saved without a last name, and no two reps can ever share the same REP_NUM. The owner asks how to enforce both without trusting whoever types the data. Which approach delivers it inside the `CREATE TABLE` statement?
options: You cannot enforce either rule in CREATE TABLE, so the program using the database has to check both
Declaring `LAST_NAME VARCHAR(15)` already forces a value, since a column with a size cannot be left empty
Listing REP_NUM first makes it the key, and every column is NOT NULL unless you say otherwise
Write `REP_NUM CHAR(2) PRIMARY KEY` and `LAST_NAME VARCHAR(15) NOT NULL` as constraints on the columns
optionNotes: Constraints like PRIMARY KEY and NOT NULL are exactly what CREATE TABLE is for, so the database enforces them itself.
VARCHAR(15) only sets a maximum length, and the column still accepts NULL until you write NOT NULL.
Column order means nothing to SQL, and columns allow NULL by default until you declare otherwise.
Correct: PRIMARY KEY blocks duplicate rep numbers and NOT NULL blocks a missing last name.
questions.takeaway: PRIMARY KEY and NOT NULL are declared with the columns in CREATE TABLE, and the engine enforces them for you.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: data types

questions.scenarioTitle: The 1,250 dollar aviary
questions.stem: An early draft of KimTay's ITEM table declares `PRICE DECIMAL(4,2)`. Before the table is ever built, a reviewer points out that KimTay is about to stock a large walk-in aviary that sells for 1250.00, and that a real MySQL server would reject that price. What is wrong with the draft, and what fixes it?
options: DECIMAL(4,2) means four digits after the decimal point, so 1250.00 already fits and something else is wrong
Change it to `DECIMAL(4,4)` so that there is room for the dollars and for the cents separately
Switch PRICE to `SMALLINT`, which holds larger numbers than any DECIMAL column is able to hold
DECIMAL(4,2) allows only four digits in total, a maximum of 99.99, so widen it to `DECIMAL(7,2)`
optionNotes: The first number is the total digit count and the second is how many of those follow the point, not an extra allowance.
DECIMAL(4,4) would put all four digits after the decimal point, leaving no room for dollars at all.
SMALLINT stores whole numbers only, so it would throw away the cents and still not solve the size problem.
Correct: DECIMAL(4,2) tops out at 99.99, while DECIMAL(7,2) reaches 99,999.99, which is the width the shipped ITEM table uses.
questions.takeaway: In DECIMAL(p,s), p is the total number of digits and s is how many of them sit after the decimal point.

questions.scenarioTitle: The same email column, three engines
questions.stem: StayWell's STUDENT table stores EMAIL as `VARCHAR(30)` in MySQL, holding values like tnguyen@example.edu. One classmate is rebuilding that table in Oracle and another is rebuilding it in Microsoft Access. What should EMAIL become in each of those two engines?
options: Oracle uses `CLOB` and Access uses Long Text, since an email address has no fixed length at all
Oracle writes it `VARCHAR2(30)` and Access calls it Short Text, the same idea under three names
Both engines take `VARCHAR(30)` unchanged, because data type names are identical in every engine
Oracle uses `NUMBER(30)` and Access uses AutoNumber, because every email address must be unique
optionNotes: CLOB and Long Text are for very long text such as paragraphs, far more than a 30-character email needs.
Correct: short text is VARCHAR(n) in MySQL, VARCHAR2(n) in Oracle and Short Text in Access.
Type names are one of the biggest differences between engines, which is why the lesson includes an equivalents table.
NUMBER holds numbers and AutoNumber generates counting ids, so neither one can store an email address.
questions.takeaway: The same concept has different names per engine: VARCHAR(n), VARCHAR2(n) and Short Text all mean short text.

questions.scenarioTitle: The two-letter state that held four
questions.stem: This page's sandbox is SQLite, which uses type affinity rather than strict checking. A classmate builds a practice table with `STATE CHAR(2)` in that sandbox, inserts the value 'Ohio', and the row is stored and displayed in full with no complaint at all. She concludes that the widths written into a CREATE TABLE statement never really matter. Why is that conclusion unsafe?
options: SQLite does not enforce a declared width, while a real MySQL or Oracle server would reject or truncate it
The sandbox actually stored the two letters Oh, and the SELECT output padded the value back out again
Widths never matter in any engine at all, so her only mistake was reading too much into the lesson
CHAR(2) limits the number of words rather than characters, and Ohio counts as a single word here
optionNotes: Correct: type affinity makes the sandbox forgiving, so a declared width is a promise you keep for the engines that do enforce it.
Nothing was trimmed; the sandbox stored all four characters, which is exactly why the row looked fine.
The lesson's own warning says an undersized column is rejected or truncated on a production MySQL or Oracle server.
A width in CHAR(n) counts characters and never words, in every engine this course covers.
questions.takeaway: The SQLite sandbox is deliberately relaxed about declared widths, so size every column for the engine that will really enforce it.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: nulls

questions.scenarioTitle: The rep the query cannot find
questions.stem: KimTay adds rep 88 to the REP table but leaves STREET out, because HR has not collected that rep's address yet. The bookkeeper runs `SELECT * FROM REP WHERE STREET = NULL;` to list reps with missing addresses and gets zero rows back. Which correction returns the new rep's row?
options: Change the condition to `WHERE STREET = '';` so that it looks for a blank street value instead
Change the condition to `WHERE STREET IS NULL;`, the only test that matches an unknown value
Change the condition to `WHERE STREET = 'NULL';` with the word NULL written inside quote marks
Change the equals sign into a double equals sign, giving `WHERE STREET == NULL;` in its place
optionNotes: An empty string is a real value stored in the column, and it is not the same thing as an unknown value.
Correct: IS NULL is the only test that matches a row whose value is unknown.
Quoting NULL turns it into the four-letter word NULL, so the query hunts for a street literally named NULL.
There is no `==` operator in standard SQL, and swapping one operator for another does not make a missing value something you can match by comparing it.
questions.takeaway: Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL to test for missing values, because = NULL never matches anything.

questions.scenarioTitle: The commission report that skips a rep
questions.stem: KimTay runs `SELECT * FROM REP WHERE COMMISSION < 30000;` to list its lower-earning reps. Rep 88 was hired this month and that row's COMMISSION is still NULL, but the row does not appear anywhere in the results. Why was it left out?
options: NULL counts as zero here, and zero is under 30000, so the row should have appeared and the query has a typo
A WHERE clause always includes NULL rows, so something else in the statement must be broken
Comparing NULL with 30000 produces UNKNOWN rather than TRUE, so the row is not returned
SQL rejected the row because NULL is text and COMMISSION is declared as a DECIMAL column
optionNotes: NULL is not zero; it means the value is unknown, so SQL will not treat it as the number 0.
A WHERE clause keeps only rows where the condition is TRUE, and UNKNOWN is not TRUE.
Correct: NULL < 30000 evaluates to UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only rows that evaluate to TRUE.
NULL has no data type of its own and is allowed in a DECIMAL column, so the column type is not the issue.
questions.takeaway: Any comparison involving NULL returns UNKNOWN, so those rows quietly drop out of a WHERE clause.

questions.scenarioTitle: Zero dollars versus no answer
questions.stem: Companion Care Clinic (customer 1310) has paid every invoice, so KimTay knows its balance is exactly 0.00. A different customer signed up this morning and nobody has worked out that account's balance yet. KimTay's bookkeeper asks how those two BALANCE values should be stored. What do you tell her?
options: Store 0.00 for the clinic and NULL for the new customer, because 0.00 is known and NULL is unknown
Store 0.00 in both rows, since NULL and zero mean exactly the same thing to the database engine
Store NULL in both rows, since neither balance has been confirmed by an actual customer payment
Store an empty string in the new customer's BALANCE so that the cell shows up blank on the report
optionNotes: Correct: 0.00 records a known balance of nothing owed, while NULL records that the balance is still unknown.
Zero is a measured amount and NULL means nobody knows yet, so storing both as 0.00 hides a real difference.
The clinic's balance is not unknown at all, since KimTay knows it is exactly zero, and NULL would lose that fact.
An empty string is text rather than a number, and it is still a stored value, not a statement that the value is unknown.
questions.takeaway: 0.00 means a known amount of nothing, while NULL means unknown or not applicable.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: adding rows with INSERT

questions.scenarioTitle: The rep who landed in the wrong column
questions.stem: KimTay's rep 35 is Richard Hull. Re-typing the REP rows, a student enters `INSERT INTO REP (REP_NUM, LAST_NAME, FIRST_NAME) VALUES ('Hull', '35', 'Richard');`. This page's SQLite sandbox does not enforce declared lengths, so the row is stored exactly as typed, and `SELECT * FROM REP;` shows a new row whose REP_NUM is Hull and whose LAST_NAME is 35. Why did the values land there?
options: The values fill the columns left to right, so 'Hull' went into the first column listed, REP_NUM.
SQL checks each value and routes it to the column whose data type it fits best.
The column list is only a comment, so the engine loaded the values alphabetically by column name.
The engine matched 'Hull' to LAST_NAME but then shifted the remaining values one place to the left.
optionNotes: Right - VALUES is positional: the first value goes into the first column you listed, the second into the second, and so on.
SQL never guesses from a value's contents or its type; position in your list is the only thing that decides where a value lands.
The column list is a real part of the statement and the engine follows the exact order you wrote - alphabetical order plays no part.
The engine never inspects a value and slides the rest sideways; nothing was shifted, because nothing was matched by meaning in the first place.
questions.takeaway: VALUES is positional - the nth value always goes into the nth column you listed.

questions.scenarioTitle: Sam's missing street address
questions.stem: Sam Alvarez is joining KimTay as rep 88, but his street address has not been confirmed yet. His rep number, last name and first name are all that has been entered so far, and REP declares STREET without NOT NULL. Which statement adds his row correctly and leaves STREET unknown?
options: `INSERT INTO REP VALUES ('88', 'Alvarez', 'Sam');` - supply the values you have and stop.
`INSERT INTO REP (REP_NUM, LAST_NAME, FIRST_NAME, STREET) VALUES ('88', 'Alvarez', 'Sam', 'unknown');`
`INSERT INTO REP (REP_NUM, LAST_NAME, FIRST_NAME) VALUES ('88', 'Alvarez', 'Sam');` - STREET is simply left out.
`INSERT INTO REP (REP_NUM, LAST_NAME, FIRST_NAME, STREET) VALUES ('88', 'Alvarez', 'Sam', '');`
optionNotes: Skipping the column list means you must supply a value for every one of REP's nine columns, in order, so this fails with a wrong-number-of-values error.
Typing the word unknown stores real text that later queries treat as an address, and `WHERE STREET IS NULL` will never find it.
Right - naming only the columns you have values for leaves STREET as NULL, the marker for an unknown value, and STREET is a column that allows NULL.
An empty string is a value the column really holds, and '' is not the same thing as NULL.
questions.takeaway: List only the columns you have values for; any column you leave out is set to NULL - which works only for columns that allow NULL.

questions.scenarioTitle: Two lines on the same invoice
questions.stem: KimTay is loading a fresh, empty copy of INVOICE_LINE one row at a time. The line for item CF21 on invoice 50710 is already stored, and the leash line is next: `INSERT INTO INVOICE_LINE (INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID, NUM_ORDERED, QUOTED_PRICE) VALUES ('50710', 'DG04', 2, 11.99);`. Item DG04 already exists in ITEM. On a DBMS that enforces referential integrity, what happens?
options: It is rejected, because INVOICE_NUM 50710 is already in the table and a key value cannot repeat.
It is accepted, because the key is the pair (INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID) and 50710 with DG04 is a new pair.
It is accepted, but it replaces the CF21 line instead of adding a second line to the invoice.
It is rejected until DG04 is inserted into ITEM, because ITEM_ID is a foreign key.
optionNotes: INVOICE_NUM alone is not the primary key here; only the combination of invoice number and item has to be unique.
Right - a composite primary key only forbids repeating the whole pair, which is exactly what lets one invoice list several items.
INSERT never overwrites an existing row; it either adds a new row or fails with an error.
On a DBMS that enforces referential integrity the foreign key would require DG04 to already exist in ITEM - and it does, so nothing needs to be re-inserted.
questions.takeaway: A composite primary key only forbids repeating the whole combination, not either column alone.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: reading data with SELECT

questions.scenarioTitle: The balance report for the four customers
questions.stem: KimTay's four customers have balances of 3512.50 (Access Pet Center), 1200.00 (Downtown Aquarium & Pets), 0.00 (Companion Care Clinic) and 4820.75 (Whiskers & Wags Boutique). KimTay's bookkeeper runs `SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE FROM CUSTOMER WHERE BALANCE > 1000 ORDER BY BALANCE DESC;`. What comes back?
options: All four customers with two columns, because ORDER BY re-sorts the whole table and overrides WHERE.
Three rows, but with all nine CUSTOMER columns - naming columns after SELECT only re-orders them.
Three rows and two columns, starting with Downtown Aquarium & Pets at 1200.00.
Three rows and two columns, starting with Whiskers & Wags Boutique at 4820.75.
optionNotes: WHERE runs first and removes Companion Care Clinic's 0.00 row; ORDER BY only arranges the rows that already survived.
The list after SELECT decides which columns appear - ask for two columns and you get exactly those two.
DESC means descending, largest first, so 1200.00 is the last row here rather than the first.
Right - WHERE keeps the three balances above 1000, the SELECT list limits output to two columns, and DESC puts the largest balance on top.
questions.takeaway: WHERE picks the rows, the SELECT list picks the columns, and ORDER BY DESC puts the largest value first.

questions.scenarioTitle: Rep 20's customer list, in alphabetical order
questions.stem: Valerie Kaiser is rep 20, and two KimTay customers are assigned to her. The bookkeeper needs just those two customer names, listed alphabetically. Which statement produces that?
options: `SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NAME WHERE REP_NUM = '20';`
`SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = '20' ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NAME;`
`SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME FROM REP WHERE REP_NUM = '20' ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NAME;`
`SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = '20';`
optionNotes: The clauses have a fixed order - SELECT, FROM, WHERE, then ORDER BY - so this is a syntax error, not just odd style.
Right - FROM picks the table, WHERE keeps only rep 20's customers, and ORDER BY puts those names in alphabetical order.
REP stores the reps themselves and has no CUSTOMER_NAME column; customer names live in the CUSTOMER table.
Without ORDER BY the engine may return rows in any order; alphabetical output is never guaranteed by default.
questions.takeaway: Clause order is fixed - SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY - and without ORDER BY no order is guaranteed.

questions.scenarioTitle: The customer that never shows up
questions.stem: The developer building KimTay's invoice report runs `SELECT i.INVOICE_NUM, c.CUSTOMER_NAME FROM INVOICE i JOIN CUSTOMER c ON i.CUSTOMER_NUM = c.CUSTOMER_NUM;`. KimTay's three invoices belong to customers 1120, 1420 and 1225; customer 1310 (Companion Care Clinic) has never been invoiced. Which customer names appear in the result?
options: Access Pet Center, Whiskers & Wags Boutique and Downtown Aquarium & Pets - the three customers that have a matching invoice.
All four customer names, because CUSTOMER is joined in and every one of its rows is available.
Only Companion Care Clinic, because it is the row the ON condition could not match.
None of them - CUSTOMER_NAME is not stored in INVOICE, so the column comes back blank.
optionNotes: Right - the ON condition produces one row per match, and Companion Care Clinic has no invoice to match, so it produces no row at all.
Being joined in makes CUSTOMER's columns available, but a customer row still has to match an invoice row to appear.
It is the opposite: an unmatched row is the one row that does NOT survive the join.
Once CUSTOMER is joined in, all of its columns are usable in SELECT - the name comes from the matched CUSTOMER row.
questions.takeaway: A JOIN keeps only the rows the ON condition can match - a customer with no invoice simply does not appear.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: fixing data safely

questions.scenarioTitle: The 500 dollars that came off every account
questions.stem: Access Pet Center paid down 500 dollars. Meaning to update only customer 1120, a clerk runs `UPDATE CUSTOMER SET BALANCE = BALANCE - 500;`. The clerk then runs `SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE FROM CUSTOMER;` to check the work. What does that SELECT show?
options: Only Access Pet Center's balance is lower, because the engine stops at the first row that fits.
All four balances are 500 lower than before, so Companion Care Clinic now reads -500.00.
The same four balances as before - UPDATE requires a WHERE clause, so the statement was rejected.
All four balances now read 500.00, because SET assigns the number you typed.
optionNotes: An UPDATE with no WHERE has nothing to stop it, so it works through every row in the table - here, all four.
Right - no WHERE means no filter, so all four rows were changed, and 0.00 minus 500 leaves Companion Care Clinic negative.
No engine protects you here; WHERE is optional to SQL, and leaving it off is a perfectly legal statement.
`SET BALANCE = BALANCE - 500` reads each row's own balance first and subtracts from it, so values dropped rather than being replaced.
questions.takeaway: An UPDATE or DELETE with no WHERE clause applies to every row in the table.

questions.scenarioTitle: Before deleting Companion Care Clinic
questions.stem: Companion Care Clinic (customer 1310) has closed permanently, it has never been invoiced, and KimTay's bookkeeper has been asked to remove its row. Lesson 3-8's safety habit says to do one thing before running the DELETE. What is it?
options: Run `DELETE FROM CUSTOMER;` first, then re-insert the three customers that are staying.
Run `UPDATE CUSTOMER SET BALANCE = 0 WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1310';` first, since a row has to be zeroed out before it can be deleted.
Nothing - run the DELETE, and undo it if the reported row count looks wrong.
Run `SELECT * FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1310';` and check that it returns only that one row.
optionNotes: Emptying a table to remove one row risks the other three customers plus any typing mistake you make re-entering them.
No rule requires a zero balance before a delete, and this statement changes a value without removing anything - Companion Care Clinic's balance is already 0.00 anyway.
There is no undo button here - once a DELETE runs, the row is gone unless you rebuild from your saved script.
Right - testing your WHERE clause as a SELECT first shows you exactly which rows the DELETE will hit.
questions.takeaway: Test the WHERE clause as a SELECT first; there is no undo after the DELETE runs.

questions.scenarioTitle: The customer that would not delete
questions.stem: Access Pet Center is customer 1120, and invoice 50710 belongs to that customer. INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM is a foreign key pointing at CUSTOMER. A clerk runs `DELETE FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1120';` on a DBMS that enforces referential integrity - this page's SQLite sandbox does not. What does that DBMS do?
options: It deletes the customer and invoice 50710 along with it, because a foreign key always removes the rows underneath.
It deletes the customer, and invoice 50710 keeps CUSTOMER_NUM 1120 even though no such customer exists any more.
It rejects the DELETE, because invoice 50710 would be left pointing at a customer that no longer exists.
It rejects the DELETE, because a DELETE has to name every table that mentions the row.
optionNotes: Removing the child rows automatically happens only when the table was built to cascade; a plain foreign key blocks the delete instead of quietly deleting invoices.
An invoice pointing at a missing customer is exactly the broken state referential integrity exists to prevent, so the DBMS refuses rather than allowing it.
Right - the foreign key requires every INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM to match a real CUSTOMER row, so the parent row cannot go while invoice 50710 still refers to it.
A DELETE names one table; what stops this statement is the foreign key rule, not a requirement to list other tables.
questions.takeaway: With referential integrity enforced, a row that other rows still point to cannot be deleted - deal with the dependent rows first.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: saving SQL as a script

questions.scenarioTitle: The work that vanished on reload
questions.stem: A student spends an hour typing KimTay's CREATE TABLE and INSERT statements into the sandbox, then reloads the page and finds everything gone. Lesson 3-9's answer is to keep the work in a script file. What does that file actually give her?
options: A plain text .sql file of her commands that she can re-run any time to rebuild the database from nothing.
A saved copy of the rows themselves, so the data reappears even if the commands are deleted.
A stored copy of her last SELECT results that she can look at without a database.
A lock on the tables so nobody else can change them until she opens the script again.
optionNotes: Right - a script is saved text: the ordered commands that recreate the structure and the data whenever you run them.
A script stores commands, not rows; the data only comes back because re-running the INSERT statements puts it back.
Query results are output, not commands - a script holds the statements you would run to produce those results again.
Saving a file has nothing to do with who may change a table; that is a permissions question, not a script.
questions.takeaway: A script is saved commands, not saved data - re-running it rebuilds the database from nothing.

questions.scenarioTitle: The setup script that ran in the wrong order
questions.stem: A classmate's kimtay_setup.sql lists all of the INSERT statements first and all of the CREATE TABLE statements at the bottom. He runs the whole file against a brand new, empty database. What happens?
options: It runs fine - the engine reads the whole file first and creates any tables it can see will be needed.
It runs, and the rows wait in a holding area until their tables are created at the bottom.
It fails only on the last statement, because a script file is executed from the bottom upward.
It stops at the first INSERT with an error, because the table that statement targets does not exist yet.
optionNotes: An engine executes a script one statement at a time, in the order written, with no advance reading or rearranging.
There is no holding area - an INSERT that names a table which does not exist simply fails on the spot.
Scripts run top to bottom, which is exactly why structure has to be defined before data is loaded.
Right - CREATE TABLE has to come before the INSERT statements that fill it, which is why script order matters.
questions.takeaway: Scripts run top to bottom, so every CREATE TABLE must come before the INSERTs that fill it.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: finishing the KimTay schema

questions.scenarioTitle: One key made of two columns
questions.stem: The developer building KimTay's INVOICE_LINE table has typed the four columns INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID, NUM_ORDERED and QUOTED_PRICE, and now has to add the key line. KimTay's rule is that one invoice can list several different items, and one item can be sold on several different invoices. Which line inside `CREATE TABLE INVOICE_LINE` states the primary key correctly?
options: `INVOICE_NUM CHAR(5) PRIMARY KEY,` - the invoice number identifies the line.
`ITEM_ID CHAR(4) PRIMARY KEY,` - the item identifies the line.
`PRIMARY KEY (INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID),` - the pair is unique even though neither column is.
`PRIMARY KEY (INVOICE_NUM), PRIMARY KEY (ITEM_ID),` - one key declared for each of the two columns.
optionNotes: An invoice that lists several items has several lines, so INVOICE_NUM repeats and cannot identify a line on its own.
An item sold on several invoices appears on several lines, so ITEM_ID repeats too and cannot identify a line by itself.
Right - a composite primary key names both columns in one declaration, and only the combination has to be unique.
A table gets exactly one primary key; when it needs two columns, they go inside a single PRIMARY KEY declaration.
questions.takeaway: When neither column is unique on its own, name both inside one PRIMARY KEY declaration.

questions.scenarioTitle: Where the price really lives
questions.stem: ITEM lists CF21 Grain-Free Dry Food at a PRICE of 42.50. On invoice 50710, the INVOICE_LINE row for CF21 shows NUM_ORDERED 3 and QUOTED_PRICE 42.50. Which statement about those two columns is correct?
options: PRICE is the item's current list price, while QUOTED_PRICE records what that particular invoice charged.
They must always match, because QUOTED_PRICE is a copy that the engine keeps in step with PRICE.
QUOTED_PRICE is the line total, so it should read 127.50 for three bags at 42.50 each.
The columns are in the wrong tables - PRICE belongs in INVOICE_LINE and QUOTED_PRICE belongs in ITEM.
optionNotes: Right - storing the quoted price on the line means a later price change in ITEM does not rewrite what an old invoice charged.
Nothing keeps the two in step; they are equal here only because this customer paid list price that day.
The line total is QUOTED_PRICE times NUM_ORDERED, worked out when needed - the column itself holds a per-item price.
Each column sits where it belongs: a list price describes the item, and a quoted price describes one line on one invoice.
questions.takeaway: ITEM.PRICE is today's list price; INVOICE_LINE.QUOTED_PRICE is what one invoice actually charged.

questions.scenarioTitle: The CREATE TABLE that returned nothing
questions.stem: Working in a brand new, empty database that holds no KimTay tables yet, the developer runs the `CREATE TABLE ITEM` statement and the output area comes back empty, with no error message. Running `SELECT * FROM ITEM;` next returns the column headings with no rows underneath them. What does that tell the developer?
options: The CREATE TABLE failed, because a statement that worked always returns at least one row.
The table exists and already holds the five KimTay items, but they stay hidden until they are inserted again.
The statement is still running, and the rows will fill in once it finishes.
The table exists and is empty - CREATE TABLE builds the structure, and no rows have been inserted yet.
optionNotes: CREATE TABLE reports success without returning rows, so an empty output area with no error is not a failure message.
Nothing is hidden - in a brand new database, rows exist only after INSERT statements put them there, which is the next step in the lesson.
These statements finish before the output appears; there is no partial result waiting to fill itself in.
Right - CREATE TABLE creates structure only, and headings with no rows underneath is exactly what a brand new empty table looks like.
questions.takeaway: CREATE TABLE builds an empty structure - column headings with no rows means the table exists and is waiting for INSERTs.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: describing a table

questions.scenarioTitle: The DESCRIBE that did not work here
questions.stem: Lesson 3-11 lists the describe command engine by engine: `DESCRIBE tablename;` in MySQL and Oracle, `sp_help tablename` in SQL Server, and `PRAGMA table_info(tablename);` in SQLite. A student who learned MySQL types `DESCRIBE CUSTOMER;` into this course's sandbox and gets an error, because the sandbox on this page is SQLite. She wants CUSTOMER's column names, their declared types, and which column is the primary key. What should she run instead?
options: `SHOW COLUMNS FROM CUSTOMER;` - the one command every database engine accepts.
`SELECT * FROM CUSTOMER;` - the headings across the top of the result are the structure.
`sp_help CUSTOMER` - the SQL Server wording, which the lesson's table shows works everywhere.
`PRAGMA table_info(CUSTOMER);` - SQLite's version of the same command.
optionNotes: SHOW COLUMNS is another MySQL wording, and it is not in the lesson's table at all - the whole point is that each engine words this differently.
SELECT * shows column names and data, but not the declared types and not which column is the primary key.
The lesson's table shows the opposite: sp_help is the SQL Server row only, and it is not what a SQLite sandbox accepts.
Right - this page's sandbox is SQLite, and `PRAGMA table_info(CUSTOMER);` is the SQLite row of the lesson's table.
questions.takeaway: Every engine words the describe command differently - DESCRIBE in MySQL and Oracle, sp_help in SQL Server, PRAGMA table_info in SQLite - so match the command to the engine you are on.

questions.scenarioTitle: Reading the output for INVOICE_LINE
questions.stem: In the SQLite sandbox, `PRAGMA table_info(INVOICE_LINE);` returns one row per column, with fields for position, name, declared type, whether the column is NOT NULL, its default value, and a pk field. Which part of that output shows the primary key is made of two columns?
options: Two of the rows have a non-zero value in the pk field: INVOICE_NUM and ITEM_ID.
Those two columns are printed first, and key columns are always listed at the top.
INVOICE_NUM and ITEM_ID are the only CHAR columns, and key columns are always text.
You should read the NOT NULL field instead, because a key column is simply a column that cannot be NULL.
optionNotes: Right - the pk field is the one that reports key membership, and a non-zero value on two rows means a two-column key.
Position only reflects the order the columns were declared; a key column can sit anywhere in the list.
Data type has nothing to do with keys - over in StayWell, PAYMENT's key is a plain number rather than text.
NOT NULL only says a value is required, and CUSTOMER_NAME is NOT NULL without being a key; in SQLite a key column can even show 0 in that field unless NOT NULL was declared explicitly.
questions.takeaway: In PRAGMA table_info output, the pk field - not position, data type, or NOT NULL - tells you which columns form the key.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: Module 3 key terms

questions.scenarioTitle: Sorting the morning's commands
questions.stem: The developer setting up KimTay's database ran four statements this morning: `CREATE TABLE ITEM (...)`, `INSERT INTO ITEM (...)`, `UPDATE ITEM SET PRICE = 44.00 WHERE ITEM_ID = 'CF21';` and `SELECT * FROM ITEM;`. Using this course's definitions, how do those four sort into DDL and DML?
options: The CREATE and the INSERT are both DDL, because each one puts something into the database that was not there before.
The CREATE, INSERT and UPDATE are DDL, and only the SELECT is DML, because the other three change something.
The CREATE is DDL; the INSERT, UPDATE and SELECT are all DML.
Only the SELECT is DML, because DML means the commands that read data out of tables.
optionNotes: INSERT adds a row of data, not a piece of structure - what a command touches, not whether it adds something, decides the category.
Changing things is not the test; an UPDATE edits values inside a table, which makes it DML no matter how much it changes.
Right - DDL is Data Definition Language and defines structure (CREATE TABLE), while DML is Data Manipulation Language and works with the data (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE).
Reading is only part of DML - INSERT and UPDATE are DML as well, even though they change data rather than read it.
questions.takeaway: DDL defines structure (CREATE TABLE); DML works with the data inside it (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE).

questions.scenarioTitle: The blank street address
questions.stem: CUSTOMER declares CUSTOMER_NAME as NOT NULL, and a new customer is entered whose STREET is not yet known, so STREET is left NULL. Which sentence uses this course's key terms correctly?
options: NULL is a constraint you put on a column so that the column is allowed to hold zero.
NOT NULL is a constraint - a rule on the column - and NULL is the marker meaning the value is unknown.
NOT NULL means the column must hold something other than an empty string.
Two customers that both have NULL in STREET are equal on that column, since NULL equals NULL.
optionNotes: NULL is not a rule and not zero - it is the marker for an unknown or not-applicable value, while NOT NULL is the constraint.
Right - a constraint is a rule enforced on a column, and NULL is the marker for a value that is unknown or does not apply.
NOT NULL only requires that a value be present; an empty string counts as a value and would be accepted.
NULL is never equal to anything, including another NULL - comparing them gives UNKNOWN, which is why IS NULL exists.
questions.takeaway: A constraint is a rule on a column; NULL is a marker for unknown and never equals anything.

matchers.heading: Match the command to what it does to the data
matchers.prompt: KimTay runs eight statements in one afternoon. Click a statement, then click the zone that describes what it does.

zones.label: Adds new rows
zones.hint: Something is in the table that was not there before

zones.label: Reads rows without changing them
zones.hint: Output only - nothing stored is altered

zones.label: Removes whole rows
zones.hint: Rows disappear; the table itself stays

cards.text: `INSERT INTO REP (REP_NUM, LAST_NAME, FIRST_NAME) VALUES ('88', 'Alvarez', 'Sam');`
cards.why: INSERT is the Create in CRUD - it puts a brand new row into a table that already exists.

cards.text: `INSERT INTO ITEM (ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, CATEGORY, ON_HAND, PRICE, REORDER_LEVEL) VALUES ('WT30', 'Ceramic Water Bowl', 'Accessory', 40, 8.75, 10);`
cards.why: A sixth product row appears in ITEM; the table's columns are exactly as they were.

cards.text: `SELECT * FROM CUSTOMER;` shows all four KimTay customers on screen
cards.why: SELECT is the Read in CRUD; it returns rows and changes nothing.

cards.text: `SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = '65';`
cards.why: A WHERE clause narrows what comes back, but a SELECT still only looks - Whiskers & Wags Boutique is displayed, not altered.

cards.text: `UPDATE CUSTOMER SET BALANCE = BALANCE - 500 WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1120';`
cards.why: UPDATE edits a value inside a row that already exists; Access Pet Center's row stays where it is.

cards.text: `UPDATE ITEM SET PRICE = 44.00 WHERE ITEM_ID = 'CF21';`
cards.why: The CF21 row keeps its place in ITEM - only the number stored in PRICE changes.

cards.text: `DELETE FROM REP WHERE REP_NUM = '88';`
cards.why: DELETE takes the whole row out, while REP itself and its other rows are untouched.

cards.text: `DELETE FROM INVOICE_LINE WHERE INVOICE_NUM = '50712' AND ITEM_ID = 'AV07';`
cards.why: Both key columns are named, so exactly one invoice line disappears and invoice 50712 keeps its FT88 line.

matchers.heading: Match each fragment to the clause it belongs in
matchers.prompt: These fragments all come from queries against KimTay's CUSTOMER table and from this lesson's INVOICE JOIN CUSTOMER report. Click a fragment, then click the clause where it belongs.

zones.label: SELECT
zones.hint: Which columns come back, and what they are headed

zones.label: FROM
zones.hint: Which table or tables to read, including a JOIN

zones.label: ORDER BY
zones.hint: What order the surviving rows appear in

cards.text: `CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE` - the two pieces of each row you want displayed
cards.why: The SELECT clause is the list of columns the result will show.

cards.text: `CUSTOMER` - the table these rows are pulled out of
cards.why: FROM names the table the query reads.

cards.text: `BALANCE > 3000` - keeps Access Pet Center and Whiskers & Wags Boutique, drops the other two
cards.why: WHERE is the test each row must pass to stay in the result.

cards.text: `CREDIT_LIMIT DESC` - puts Companion Care Clinic's 10000.00 first and Downtown Aquarium & Pets' 5000.00 last
cards.why: DESC appears only in ORDER BY; it arranges the rows the query already found, largest value first.

cards.text: `CREDIT_LIMIT AS CREDIT_CEILING` - gives an output column a friendlier heading
cards.why: An AS alias renames a column in the output list, so it belongs with SELECT.

cards.text: `CITY = 'Maple Grove'` - narrows the list to two of the four customers
cards.why: It is a test applied to each row, so it belongs with the other WHERE conditions.

cards.text: `INVOICE i JOIN CUSTOMER c ON i.CUSTOMER_NUM = c.CUSTOMER_NUM` - the two tables the invoice report reads, and how their rows line up
cards.why: A JOIN is written as part of FROM: it names the second table and the ON condition that matches rows to rows.

matchers.heading: Match each message or symptom to what went wrong
matchers.prompt: Seven things a student saw on screen while building the KimTay tables from her own script. Click a message or symptom, then click the cause that explains it.

zones.label: Wrong number of values
zones.hint: The VALUES list does not line up with the columns

zones.label: Primary key value already used
zones.hint: That key value is already stored

zones.label: Table name not found
zones.hint: The engine cannot find the name you typed

zones.label: No WHERE clause
zones.hint: The statement reached every row in the table

zones.label: Required column left out
zones.hint: A NOT NULL column was given no value

cards.text: `table REP has 9 columns but 3 values were supplied`
cards.why: The INSERT skipped the column list, so all nine REP columns need a value, in order.

cards.text: `INSERT INTO CUSTOMER (CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME) VALUES ('1500', 'Paws and Claws Grooming', 4000.00);`
cards.why: Two columns are named but three values are supplied, so the two lists cannot line up.

cards.text: `UNIQUE constraint failed: REP.REP_NUM` when you re-run only the INSERT half of your script against tables that already hold those rows
cards.why: The rows are already there, so inserting the same REP_NUM again collides with the primary key - re-run the whole script against an empty database instead.

cards.text: `no such table: CUSTOMR` at the end of a long typing session
