cards.text: Every item's PRICE reads 19.99 after one UPDATE
cards.why: `UPDATE ITEM SET PRICE = 19.99;` rewrote all five item rows; naming one ITEM_ID would have limited it.

cards.text: After one DELETE, `SELECT * FROM INVOICE_LINE;` returns zero rows
cards.why: `DELETE FROM INVOICE_LINE;` empties the whole table; a WHERE naming the invoice and item removes a single line.

cards.text: `INSERT INTO REP (REP_NUM, FIRST_NAME) VALUES ('90', 'Dana');` reports `NOT NULL constraint failed: REP.LAST_NAME`
cards.why: Two columns named and two values supplied, so the counts line up - what failed is that LAST_NAME is declared NOT NULL and was left out entirely.

quizzes.heading: Module 2 cumulative review: design, keys, and normal forms

questions.scenarioTitle: The cell with two dates in it
questions.stem: StayWell's office assistant keeps a lease spreadsheet in which the row for student Trang Nguyen lists PAYMENT_DATES as "2026-08-01, 2026-09-01" inside a single cell. The assistant asks whether that is acceptable before the sheet is loaded into the real database. Which answer is correct?
options: It breaks 2NF, because the payment dates depend on only part of a composite key
It is acceptable as long as the dates are kept in order, since each one is still readable
It breaks 1NF, and the fix is to give each payment its own row in a separate PAYMENT table
It breaks 3NF, because PAYMENT_DATES depends on another non-key column instead of on the key
optionNotes: A partial dependency is a 2NF problem and requires a composite key; here the problem is a list crammed into one cell, which is 1NF's job.
Readable is not the same as atomic - a comma-separated list forces you to pick text apart instead of querying rows, which is what 1NF forbids.

First Normal Form requires one atomic value per cell, and giving each payment its own row in PAYMENT is exactly the 1NF fix this module walks through - which is why lease L001 shows up as two PAYMENT rows, not one cell with two dates.
A transitive dependency is a 3NF problem about one non-key column determining another, and nothing here depends on another non-key column.
questions.takeaway: Multiple values stuffed into one cell is a repeating group, and repeating groups are always a 1NF violation.

questions.scenarioTitle: The item description that rode along on every line
questions.stem: KimTay's bookkeeper builds a reporting table whose primary key is (INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID) and which also stores NUM_ORDERED and DESCRIPTION. DESCRIPTION depends only on ITEM_ID, so "Grain-Free Dry Food 30lb" is retyped on invoice 50710 and again on invoice 50711, the two invoices that both sell CF21. Which statement names the violation and its fix?
options: 2NF is violated; moving DESCRIPTION into ITEM leaves ITEM_ID behind in the line table as a foreign key
Nothing is violated, because DESCRIPTION is not part of the primary key and only key columns get checked
1NF is violated, because it takes two columns together to identify a single row
3NF is violated, because DESCRIPTION depends on ITEM_ID, which is a non-key column
optionNotes: DESCRIPTION depends on part of the composite key, which is a partial dependency, and pulling it into ITEM turns ITEM_ID into a foreign key pointing at ITEM.
Normal forms are entirely about how the non-key columns depend on the key, so the non-key columns are exactly what you examine.
A composite key is perfectly legal in 1NF; 1NF only cares that every cell holds a single atomic value.
ITEM_ID is half of the primary key, not a non-key column, so this is a partial dependency (2NF), not a transitive one.
questions.takeaway: Depends on part of a composite key means 2NF; depends on a non-key column means 3NF.

questions.scenarioTitle: The rep name copied onto forty rows
questions.stem: Suppose KimTay grows well past its four sample customers to several hundred, with rep Juan Perez working with forty of them. A new sales analyst builds a wide mailing-list table with one row per customer, keyed on CUSTOMER_NUM alone, that also stores REP_NUM and REP_LAST_NAME. Correcting the spelling of Perez's last name now means editing forty separate rows. What is wrong, and what does fixing it create?
options: REP_LAST_NAME depends on only part of the key, so 2NF is violated and the key must be widened
REP_LAST_NAME depends on REP_NUM, which violates 3NF; splitting the rep facts into REP leaves REP_NUM behind as a foreign key
Nothing is wrong, because repeating one rep's name across many rows is normal in a relational database
The table needs the composite key (CUSTOMER_NUM, REP_NUM) so that the rep's name is stored only once
optionNotes: CUSTOMER_NUM is a single-column key, and a single-column key has no parts, so a partial dependency is impossible here.
A non-key column determining another non-key column is a transitive dependency, and moving rep facts into REP leaves the mailing-list table holding only the REP_NUM foreign key.
Those forty copies of one name are precisely the update anomaly normalization exists to remove - one real-world change should require one edit.
Adding columns to the key does not remove the duplication; it only makes the key bigger while the name still repeats on every row.
questions.takeaway: A non-key column that depends on another non-key column is a 3NF violation, and the fix always leaves a new foreign key behind.

questions.scenarioTitle: The description that wanted to be the key
questions.stem: KimTay's ITEM table uses ITEM_ID as its primary key, and a catalog rule guarantees that no two items ever share a DESCRIPTION and that a description is never left blank. The developer drafting next year's schema proposes identifying items by DESCRIPTION instead of ITEM_ID. Which response is correct?
options: DESCRIPTION cannot be a key, because primary keys have to be short codes or numbers like CF21
DESCRIPTION is a foreign key, since the wording is copied straight from the supplier's printed catalog
Only one column per table is allowed to be unique, so DESCRIPTION must already contain duplicates
DESCRIPTION is a candidate key and could serve as the key, but INVOICE_LINE already references ITEM_ID as a foreign key
optionNotes: Nothing about a key requires a short or numeric value; a key only has to be unique and never null for every row.
A foreign key references the primary key of another table inside this database, not a document from outside it.
Any number of columns may be unique, and every column that is unique and non-null counts as a candidate key.
Both columns qualify as candidate keys, but the primary key is the one foreign keys elsewhere point at, so swapping it means rewriting INVOICE_LINE too.
questions.takeaway: A table can have several candidate keys, but the primary key is the one the rest of the schema references.

questions.scenarioTitle: The duplicate room number
questions.stem: StayWell's ROOM table holds Room 101 at Millbrook Commons (P100) and Room 101 at Sycamore Court (P200) - the same room number in two different buildings. Suppose the designer had made ROOM_NUM alone the primary key of ROOM. What would happen when the second of those rooms was inserted, and why is (PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM) the right key?
options: The insert succeeds and quietly overwrites the Millbrook Commons row that already used 101
The insert is rejected because a primary key value cannot repeat, and the pair is unique even when room numbers are not
The insert succeeds, because entity integrity only forbids a primary key from being NULL
The insert is rejected because ROOM_NUM is a foreign key that must match a row in PROPERTY
optionNotes: A primary key conflict never overwrites an existing row; the database refuses the new row and reports an error instead.
Entity integrity means every primary key value is unique and non-null, and pairing the room number with the property makes (P100,101) and (P200,101) two distinct keys.
Entity integrity has two halves - never NULL and never duplicated - and this insert breaks the second half.
ROOM_NUM is part of ROOM's own primary key, not a foreign key; only PROPERTY_ID references PROPERTY.
questions.takeaway: Use a composite key whenever one column's values legitimately repeat across rows that are genuinely different things.

questions.scenarioTitle: The city that looked like a determinant
questions.stem: Looking at KimTay's four sample customers, a classmate notices that the two Maple Grove rows both show STATE 'OH' and that the Northfield and Brookville rows do too. He writes down CITY -> STATE as a functional dependency. Why is that a mistake?
options: It is not a mistake, because the sample data shows the dependency holding for every row
It is a mistake only because CITY is not the primary key, and only primary keys can be determinants
A functional dependency must hold for every row the business could ever store, and Springfield exists in several states
It is a mistake because STATE is a CHAR(2) column, and short columns can never be dependents
optionNotes: A small sample can make an accident look like a rule, which is the exact warning this module gives about the Maple Grove rows.
Any column can be a determinant - ZIP determines CITY and STATE without being anybody's primary key.
Functional dependence is a business rule about all possible data, and Springfield, OH plus Springfield, IL breaks CITY -> STATE immediately.
Data type has nothing to do with dependency; a two-character column can be determined by another column perfectly well.
questions.takeaway: A functional dependency is a rule about every row the business could ever store, not a pattern you spotted in the sample.

questions.scenarioTitle: We can normalize it later
questions.stem: KimTay's sales manager asks for one wide table holding customer name, rep name, item description, and quantity, saying the team can clean it up after go-live. Measured against the four design phases in this module - requirements, conceptual design, logical design with normalization, and physical design - what actually went wrong?
options: Physical design was skipped, so the table will be created with no data types on its columns
Requirements gathering was skipped, so nobody knows which columns the business actually needs
Nothing went wrong, because a single wide table is exactly what physical design is supposed to produce
Conceptual design and normalization were skipped, so redundancy and update anomalies come straight back
optionNotes: Physical design is the last phase, where data types and storage details get chosen, and it is not what this shortcut skipped.
The manager did state a requirement; what he skipped was turning it into entities, relationships, and normalized tables.
Physical design implements an already normalized logical design - it does not invent a flat spreadsheet.
Jumping straight to a table skips the ER diagram and the 1NF to 2NF to 3NF pass, which is how the anomalies from Lesson 1-1 get back in.
questions.takeaway: The four phases are requirements, conceptual design, logical design with normalization, and physical design, and skipping the two middle phases is what reintroduces anomalies.

questions.scenarioTitle: Reading the KimTay diagram out loud
questions.stem: On KimTay's ER diagram the CUSTOMER box lists CUSTOMER_NUM in bold underline on its first line and REP_NUM in italics on its last line. The line joining CUSTOMER to REP carries the exactly-one symbol (two short tick marks, no circle) at the REP end and a crow's foot at the CUSTOMER end. What business rule is drawn there?
options: Each customer has many reps, and each rep is tied to exactly one customer
Each customer has exactly one rep, one rep serves many customers, and CUSTOMER.REP_NUM is the foreign key
CUSTOMER_NUM and REP_NUM together form CUSTOMER's composite primary key
REP_NUM is italic to show that it is optional and may be left blank on any customer row
optionNotes: That reads the symbols backwards: the two tick marks sit on the REP end, so it is the rep side that is limited to exactly one.
Two tick marks with no circle mean exactly one, a crow's foot means many, and the italic REP_NUM on CUSTOMER's last line is the foreign key that physically carries the relationship.
Bold underline marks the primary key and italics mark a foreign key, so REP_NUM is a reference rather than part of CUSTOMER's key.
Italics mean foreign key in this course's diagrams; optionality is shown with a circle on the relationship line, not with italics.
questions.takeaway: Bold underline is the primary key, italics is the foreign key, and the symbols on each line end tell you how many rows sit on that side.

questions.scenarioTitle: Nesting the lines inside the invoices
questions.stem: A study partner suggests KimTay could skip the relational model and store everything as a strict hierarchy, with each invoice owning its lines the way a folder owns its files. You point at item CF21: the Grain-Free Dry Food appears on invoice 50710 and again on invoice 50711, and each of those invoices also lists a second item. Why does that sink the hierarchy?
options: An item appears on many invoices and an invoice lists many items, so neither one can be the single parent
A hierarchical structure cannot store more than one level of child records below the top
The hierarchical model has no way to store numeric columns such as QUOTED_PRICE
The relational model also requires one parent per row, so both models fail on this data
optionNotes: A strict tree gives every child exactly one parent, and a many-to-many relationship has no single parent, which is why INVOICE_LINE exists in the relational design with ITEM on one side and INVOICE on the other.
Hierarchies handle many levels perfectly well; the real limit is one parent per child.
Storing numbers is not the issue - the issue is the shape of the relationship between the records.
The relational model connects tables by matching key values, so a connecting table like INVOICE_LINE resolves many-to-many cleanly.
questions.takeaway: Many-to-many relationships break a strict hierarchy, and a connecting table with a composite key is the relational answer.

questions.scenarioTitle: The property that disappeared
questions.stem: StayWell's old flat report kept one row per lease, and every row also carried the property's name, address, and manager. Riverbend Hall appears on exactly one of those rows. That student's lease ends, the row is deleted, and now nothing in the database records that Riverbend Hall exists at all. Name the problem and the fix.
options: An insertion anomaly, because deleting a row is really the same thing as failing to insert one
An update anomaly, because the property manager's name would have to be corrected on every other row too
A deletion anomaly; moving property facts into their own PROPERTY table keeps them independent of any student
No anomaly at all, since a property with no students living in it does not need to be stored
optionNotes: An insertion anomaly is the opposite problem: not being able to add a new property until some student lives there.
An update anomaly is having to repeat the same edit across many rows, but here the fact vanished entirely instead.
Losing an unrelated fact as a side effect of deleting a row is the deletion anomaly, and a separate PROPERTY table stores that fact on its own row.
StayWell absolutely needs to know about a vacant property so it can advertise and lease those rooms.
questions.takeaway: Insertion, update, and deletion anomalies are three different symptoms, and each one disappears once every fact lives in its own table.

quizzes.heading: Module 3 cumulative review: writing and reading SQL

questions.scenarioTitle: The query that came back empty
questions.stem: KimTay's four sample customers carry balances of 3512.50, 1200.00, 0.00, and 4820.75. A clerk runs `SELECT * FROM CUSTOMER WHERE BALANCE > 5000;` and stares at a blank result. What actually happened?
options: All four rows should have come back, because a WHERE clause on a DECIMAL column always matches
Zero rows is correct, because no customer balance in the sample is greater than 5000
Whiskers and Wags Boutique should appear, because 4820.75 rounds up to 5000
The statement fails, because the number in a WHERE clause must be quoted as '5000'
optionNotes: WHERE filters rows by testing the condition against each one; it does not pass everything through.
The largest balance in the sample is 4820.75, so nothing satisfies BALANCE > 5000 and an empty result is the right answer; the statement ran perfectly well.
SQL compares the stored value exactly as it is and never rounds it to make a comparison succeed.
Numeric literals are written without quotes; quoting turns 5000 into text, which is a different kind of comparison.
questions.takeaway: An empty result usually means your condition worked correctly and nothing matched, not that the query is broken.

questions.scenarioTitle: The rep with no street address
questions.stem: A new rep is added with `INSERT INTO REP (REP_NUM, LAST_NAME, FIRST_NAME) VALUES ('88', 'Alvarez', 'Sam');`, so STREET and COMMISSION are both left out of the statement and land in the row as NULL. Afterward `SELECT * FROM REP WHERE STREET = NULL;` returns no rows at all, while `SELECT COMMISSION + 100 FROM REP WHERE REP_NUM = '88';` returns one row containing NULL. Which single explanation covers both results?
options: The INSERT never really ran, so there is no row 88 for either statement to find
NULL is stored as an empty string, so `WHERE STREET = ''` would work and the arithmetic should return 100
The DBMS ignores WHERE clauses that mention columns left out of the INSERT statement
Any comparison or arithmetic touching NULL yields UNKNOWN or NULL, so you must test with `IS NULL`
optionNotes: The row does exist - the second statement found it and returned a row, which is why you got a NULL result rather than no rows at all.
NULL means unknown and is not an empty string, a zero, or a blank; an empty string is a real value somebody actually typed.
WHERE is always evaluated, but `STREET = NULL` produces UNKNOWN, and a WHERE clause treats UNKNOWN as not matching.
Three-valued logic means NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN instead of TRUE, and an unknown commission plus 100 is still unknown, so `WHERE STREET IS NULL` is the only way to find the row.
questions.takeaway: NULL is unknown, so it never equals anything and never survives arithmetic - use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL.

questions.scenarioTitle: Who is the Whiskers and Wags rep?
questions.stem: The sales manager wants one list showing every KimTay customer's name beside their rep's last name. CUSTOMER stores only REP_NUM, while the names live in REP. Which statement produces that list?
options: `SELECT c.CUSTOMER_NAME, r.LAST_NAME FROM CUSTOMER c JOIN REP r ON c.REP_NUM = r.REP_NUM;`
`SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, LAST_NAME FROM CUSTOMER, REP;`
`SELECT c.CUSTOMER_NAME, r.LAST_NAME FROM CUSTOMER c JOIN REP r ON c.CUSTOMER_NUM = r.REP_NUM;`
`SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, LAST_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM IS NOT NULL;`
optionNotes: The ON clause pairs each customer with the one REP row sharing its REP_NUM, which is exactly the foreign-key relationship a join follows.
Naming two tables with no matching condition pairs every customer with every rep, producing twelve nonsense rows instead of four.
Joining CUSTOMER_NUM to REP_NUM compares unrelated values; ON must compare the foreign key to the key it actually references.
CUSTOMER has no LAST_NAME column at all, so no WHERE clause can make a rep's name appear without joining REP.
questions.takeaway: A JOIN needs an ON clause that equates the foreign key with the primary key it references.

questions.scenarioTitle: How many rows should come back?
questions.stem: KimTay has three invoices and six INVOICE_LINE rows, two lines on each invoice. A clerk runs `SELECT i.INVOICE_NUM, l.ITEM_ID FROM INVOICE i JOIN INVOICE_LINE l ON i.INVOICE_NUM = l.INVOICE_NUM;`. How many rows come back?
options: Three, because a JOIN collapses the matching lines back into one row per invoice
Nine, because the join returns the three invoices plus the six lines counted together
Six, because a JOIN produces one row for every matching invoice-and-line pair
Eighteen, because each of the three invoices is paired with each of the six lines
optionNotes: An invoice with two lines appears twice in the output; the join repeats the INVOICE row once per matching line.
A join does not stack two tables end to end, so you count matching pairs rather than adding the two row counts together.
One output row per matching pair means all six INVOICE_LINE rows find their invoice, giving six rows.
Pairing everything with everything is what happens when you leave the ON clause off, not when you supply one.
questions.takeaway: A JOIN returns one row per matching pair, so the many side usually decides the row count.

questions.scenarioTitle: The 500 dollars that came off every account
questions.stem: A KimTay clerk meant to credit Access Pet Center for a 500 dollar payment, but typed `UPDATE CUSTOMER SET BALANCE = BALANCE - 500;` and pressed Run. What happened, and what habit prevents it next time?
options: Every customer's balance dropped by 500; write the WHERE clause as a SELECT first and check what it matches
Nothing happened, because an UPDATE with no WHERE clause is rejected as a syntax error
Only the first row changed, because UPDATE stops as soon as it has modified one row
Only Access Pet Center changed, because the DBMS reuses the row from the previous SELECT
optionNotes: Running `SELECT * FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1120';` first proves the filter matches only the intended row before you change anything.
The statement is perfectly valid SQL, which is exactly why it is dangerous - the database runs it without complaint.
UPDATE changes every row that satisfies the WHERE clause, and with no WHERE clause every row satisfies it.
A DBMS keeps no memory of your previous SELECT; each statement stands entirely on its own.
questions.takeaway: UPDATE and DELETE with no WHERE clause hit every row, so always test the filter with a SELECT first.

questions.scenarioTitle: The cheap, well-stocked restock list
questions.stem: KimTay's buyer wants a short restock list: every item priced under 30 dollars that also has at least 25 units on hand, most expensive first. ITEM holds Aviary Starter Cage (64.99, 15 on hand), Grain-Free Dry Food 30lb (42.50, 48), Nylon Dog Leash 6ft (11.99, 120), Fish Tank Filter Kit (27.75, 30), and Small Animal Grooming Kit (15.25, 22). Which statement produces the list?
options: `SELECT DESCRIPTION, PRICE FROM ITEM WHERE PRICE < 30 OR ON_HAND >= 25 ORDER BY PRICE DESC;`
`SELECT DESCRIPTION, PRICE FROM ITEM ORDER BY PRICE DESC WHERE PRICE < 30 AND ON_HAND >= 25;`
`SELECT DESCRIPTION, PRICE FROM ITEM WHERE PRICE < 30 AND ON_HAND >= 25 SORT BY PRICE DESC;`
`SELECT DESCRIPTION, PRICE FROM ITEM WHERE PRICE < 30 AND ON_HAND >= 25 ORDER BY PRICE DESC;`
optionNotes: OR widens the result because a row only has to satisfy one condition, so the 42.50 dry food and the 22-unit grooming kit come back too.

ORDER BY always follows the WHERE clause. Written this way the database cannot even parse the statement: it reports a syntax error at WHERE and never runs the query, which is different from a valid query that runs and simply matches no rows.
SORT BY is not SQL - the keyword for arranging the rows you selected is ORDER BY - so the database rejects the statement with an error instead of running it and returning an empty grid.
AND requires both conditions to be true on the same row, leaving the filter kit at 27.75 and the leash at 11.99, sorted from the higher price down.
questions.takeaway: AND narrows a result while OR widens it, and the clause order is always SELECT, then FROM, then WHERE, then ORDER BY.

questions.scenarioTitle: The price that would not fit
questions.stem: KimTay's ITEM.PRICE column is declared DECIMAL(7,2). The buyer wants to add a custom aquarium priced at 129999.99 and asks whether the column can hold it, and what the same column would look like in Oracle.
options: It fits, because the 7 counts only the digits that appear before the decimal point
It fits, because DECIMAL(7,2) allows 7 digits before the point and 2 after it, so 9 in total
It does not fit; that value needs 8 digits total, and Oracle would declare the column NUMBER(7,2)
It does not fit, and Oracle has no decimal type at all, so the price must be stored as VARCHAR2
optionNotes: The first number is the total digit count, so DECIMAL(7,2) tops out at 99999.99.
That reading double counts: the precision 7 covers all digits including the 2 after the point, not 7 plus 2.
129999.99 has eight digits, which overflows DECIMAL(7,2), and Oracle's equivalent decimal type is NUMBER(p,s).
Oracle stores decimals in NUMBER(p,s); keeping money as text would break sorting and arithmetic.
questions.takeaway: In DECIMAL(p,s) the p is total digits and the s is how many of those digits fall after the decimal point.

questions.scenarioTitle: The rep whose first name became her last
questions.stem: Intending to add rep Amelia Ross, a clerk runs `INSERT INTO REP (REP_NUM, FIRST_NAME, LAST_NAME) VALUES ('72', 'Ross', 'Amelia');`. Then `SELECT * FROM REP;` shows something odd. What went wrong?
options: The DBMS matches values to columns by meaning, so the row was actually stored correctly as Amelia Ross
Values fill the columns in the order listed, so the rep is stored with FIRST_NAME 'Ross' and LAST_NAME 'Amelia'
The statement failed, because LAST_NAME and FIRST_NAME are declared NOT NULL in the REP table
The statement failed, because a column list must always repeat the table's declared column order
optionNotes: A DBMS has no idea which strings are first names; it simply lines the values up positionally against the column list.
The first value goes to the first column named and the second to the second, so swapping the names in VALUES swaps them in the stored row.
Both columns did receive a value, so the NOT NULL constraints were satisfied - the values were merely in the wrong places.
You may list the columns in any order you like, as long as the VALUES appear in that same order.
questions.takeaway: INSERT matches values to columns strictly by position, so the column list and the VALUES list must line up.

questions.scenarioTitle: The invoice for a customer who is not there
questions.stem: INVOICE was created with `FOREIGN KEY (CUSTOMER_NUM) REFERENCES CUSTOMER(CUSTOMER_NUM)`. Someone runs `INSERT INTO INVOICE VALUES ('50713', '9999', '2026-06-20');` and KimTay has no customer 9999. Assume a DBMS such as MySQL or Oracle, where referential integrity is enforced. What should the DBMS do, and why?
options: Accept it, and create a placeholder CUSTOMER row with number 9999 automatically
Accept it, because a foreign key is only checked when rows are deleted from CUSTOMER
Reject it, because CUSTOMER_NUM values have to be unique within the INVOICE table
Reject it, because the foreign key requires 9999 to already exist as a CUSTOMER_NUM in CUSTOMER
optionNotes: A foreign key constraint refuses bad values; it never invents the missing parent row on your behalf.
The constraint is checked on INSERT and UPDATE too, which is what stops orphaned invoices from ever being created.
Uniqueness is a primary key or UNIQUE rule; CUSTOMER_NUM is meant to repeat in INVOICE, because one customer has many invoices - 1120, 1420, and 1225 each own an invoice here.
A foreign key value must match an existing primary key value in the referenced table, so an invoice can never point at a customer who does not exist.
questions.takeaway: On a DBMS that enforces referential integrity, a foreign key guarantees that every reference points at a row that really exists in the referenced table.

questions.scenarioTitle: The setup script that failed halfway
questions.stem: A student saves kimtay_setup.sql with `CREATE TABLE INVOICE_LINE` first, then ITEM and INVOICE, and runs it against MySQL with `mysql -u root -p kimtay_pet_supplies < kimtay_setup.sql`. MySQL rejects the very first statement. What is wrong, and what is the fix?
options: INVOICE_LINE's foreign keys reference tables that do not exist yet, so create INVOICE and ITEM before it
A .sql script must list its CREATE TABLE statements in alphabetical order by table name
A script file can hold only one statement, so everything after the first CREATE was ignored
The script fails only because it is missing a CREATE DATABASE line, which every SQL engine requires
optionNotes: `FOREIGN KEY (ITEM_ID) REFERENCES ITEM(ITEM_ID)` cannot be honored until ITEM exists, so parent tables always come first in a setup script.
Alphabetical order is a coincidence at best; what matters is that a referenced table is created before the table that references it.
A script is simply a list of statements run in order, and running many statements at once is the whole point of saving one.
The database kimtay_pet_supplies already exists here - it is named on the command line - and not every engine even has CREATE DATABASE, since in SQLite the database is simply the file you open.
questions.takeaway: In a setup script, create the tables a foreign key points at before the tables that point at them.

matchers.heading: Cumulative match-up: Module 2 vocabulary in the real schemas
matchers.prompt: Click a card, then click the term it belongs to. Every card fits exactly one term - if two look possible, re-read what the card says the column or symbol actually does.

zones.label: Foreign key
zones.hint: one column holding another table's key

zones.label: Composite key
zones.hint: two columns needed together to identify a row

zones.label: Candidate key
zones.hint: unique and non-null, but not the column the designer chose

zones.label: Cardinality
zones.hint: how many rows may sit on each end of a relationship

zones.label: Normalization
zones.hint: splitting one wide table to kill redundancy

cards.text: CUSTOMER.REP_NUM, drawn in italics on the last line of the CUSTOMER box, whose value must already exist over in REP
cards.why: It stores another table's primary key purely to reference that row, which is why the diagram italicizes it.

cards.text: INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM, how invoice 50710 knows it belongs to Access Pet Center
cards.why: The invoice carries the customer's key instead of copying the customer's details.

cards.text: The pair (INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID) that identifies one line on one invoice
cards.why: Invoice 50710 has two lines and CF21 appears on both 50710 and 50711, so only the pair is unique.

cards.text: Neither PROPERTY_ID nor ROOM_NUM identifies a room by itself, so ROOM's key is both of them
cards.why: Room 101 exists at Millbrook Commons and again at Sycamore Court, so the property must be part of the key.

cards.text: MANAGER.PHONE, a direct line StayWell never leaves blank and never assigns to two managers, though MANAGER_ID is what PROPERTY actually references
cards.why: The stated business rule makes it unique and non-null, so it qualifies to identify rows even though MANAGER_ID was chosen as the primary key.

cards.text: The crow's foot drawn on the CUSTOMER end of the REP to CUSTOMER line
cards.why: End symbols state how many rows may sit on each side of a relationship, and a crow's foot means many.

cards.text: A circle plus one tick mark on the end of a relationship line, meaning zero or one row on that side
cards.why: The circle means the row is optional and the tick mark means there is at most one of it.

cards.text: Turning one flat lease report into MANAGER, PROPERTY, ROOM, STUDENT, LEASE, and PAYMENT
cards.why: That step-by-step split through 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF is normalization itself.

matchers.heading: Cumulative match-up: what does this SQL do to the KimTay database?
matchers.prompt: Click a statement, then click the effect it has on KimTay's data. Ask yourself one question for each: after this runs, does the table have more rows, fewer rows, different values, a brand-new definition, or no change at all?

zones.label: Defines a new table
zones.hint: a new empty structure, no rows stored

cards.text: `CREATE TABLE SUPPLIER (SUPPLIER_ID CHAR(4) PRIMARY KEY, SUPPLIER_NAME VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL);`
cards.why: CREATE TABLE is DDL: it defines an empty structure and stores no data.

cards.text: `CREATE TABLE PURCHASE_ORDER (PO_NUM CHAR(5) PRIMARY KEY, SUPPLIER_ID CHAR(4), FOREIGN KEY (SUPPLIER_ID) REFERENCES SUPPLIER(SUPPLIER_ID));`
cards.why: It defines a second empty table and the foreign key that will link it to SUPPLIER; not one row is stored yet.

cards.text: `INSERT INTO REP (REP_NUM, LAST_NAME, FIRST_NAME) VALUES ('45', 'Okafor', 'Amy');`
cards.why: INSERT is the Create in CRUD, adding one brand-new rep row to REP alongside 20, 35, and 65.

cards.text: `INSERT INTO INVOICE_LINE VALUES ('50711', 'DG04', 4, 11.99);`
cards.why: It records a new line on invoice 50711, so INVOICE_LINE goes from six rows to seven.

cards.text: `UPDATE ITEM SET PRICE = 44.95 WHERE ITEM_ID = 'CF21';`
cards.why: The Grain-Free Dry Food row stays put; only its PRICE value changes from 42.50.

cards.text: `DELETE FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1310';`
cards.why: Companion Care Clinic is removed, so CUSTOMER drops from four rows to three.

cards.text: `SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE FROM CUSTOMER WHERE BALANCE > 1000 ORDER BY BALANCE DESC;`
cards.why: SELECT is the Read in CRUD and never modifies the stored data.

cards.text: `SELECT i.INVOICE_NUM, c.CUSTOMER_NAME FROM INVOICE i JOIN CUSTOMER c ON i.CUSTOMER_NUM = c.CUSTOMER_NUM;`
cards.why: A JOIN reassembles data from two tables for display without changing either one.

quizzes.heading: Check yourself: what Supabase is and what the Free plan gives you

questions.scenarioTitle: The laptop that died on Tuesday
questions.stem: A student has been building the KimTay tables in the sandbox on this page, on whichever lab computer is free that day. Twice now the tables have disappeared after the page was reloaded, and next week they will be working from home instead. They want one place to put the tables that survives both the reload and the change of computer.
options: Keep using the in-page sandbox but simply avoid reloading the tab until the assignment is graded
Install PostgreSQL on the lab computer, so the tables are saved to disk and reachable from home
Create a Supabase project, since the database lives on Supabase's servers and opens from any browser
Copy the SQL into a text file every time, because none of the three options actually stores data
optionNotes: The sandbox is deliberately throwaway -- the page says your tables are gone the moment you reload, and a shared lab machine gets reloaded by the next student.
A local install is permanent but lives on exactly one machine, so tables written on a lab computer are simply not there when you get home.
Correct -- the page puts Supabase in between the other two: a real database that keeps your data and that you reach from any computer with a web browser.
Keeping your own copy of the SQL is good advice because the Free plan has no backups, but a local install and a Supabase project both do keep data on their own.
questions.takeaway: Sandbox for throwaway experiments, local install for one machine, Supabase when the data has to outlive the tab and the computer.

questions.scenarioTitle: The second project that would not start
questions.stem: A student already has one active Free-plan project holding KimTay and now wants a second project for a personal experiment. A classmate says to just create another organization to get more projects, and adds that the storage cap is shared between them anyway.
options: The Free plan allows 2 active projects in total across every organization where you are Owner or Administrator, so a second organization adds nothing
Each organization gets its own 2 active projects, so creating a second organization doubles the allowance
The 500 MB of storage is shared across projects, so a second project halves what KimTay can hold
Free projects are uncapped until a credit card is added, and only paid plans meter storage
optionNotes: Correct -- the page states the 2-active-project limit is a total across every organization where you are an Owner or Administrator, and that paused projects do not count against it.
This is exactly the misconception the page calls out: the limit is not two per organization, so extra organizations do not raise your total.
The 500 MB is per project, not shared, and the whole KimTay database is only a few kilobytes, so storage is never the pinch point here.
Backwards -- the Free plan is the one carrying the limits (2 active projects, 500 MB each, pausing after a week idle), and it never asks for a credit card.
questions.takeaway: Free plan: 2 active projects account-wide, 500 MB per project, no credit card -- plan on one project for KimTay and keep the other slot free.

questions.scenarioTitle: The project that went quiet over the break
questions.stem: A student returns from a two-week break, opens the Supabase dashboard, and finds the KimTay project marked as paused. Convinced a semester of work has been thrown away, they start hunting for the `CREATE TABLE` script to build everything again.
options: The tables were erased when the project paused, so the whole schema has to be rebuilt from a saved script
A paused project must be restored within seven days or Supabase discards it permanently
Only the paid plan's daily backups can revive a paused project, and the Free plan does not have them
Click the project, choose `Resume project`, confirm, and the tables and rows come back in a few minutes
optionNotes: Pausing is not deletion -- the page is explicit that tables, rows, and settings are all preserved on disk while the project is asleep.
Seven days is the inactivity window that triggers a pause, not a deadline for restoring; the page gives you a one-year window to resume from the dashboard.
Resuming has nothing to do with backups -- it is a dashboard button, and the Free plan's missing backups only matter if you damage or delete the data yourself.
Correct -- open the dashboard, click your organization, click the paused project, then `Resume project` and confirm; restoring takes a few minutes.
questions.takeaway: A pause costs you a few minutes, not your work -- and running `select 1;` once or twice a week keeps the project awake in the first place.

quizzes.heading: Check yourself: creating the project without creating a problem

questions.scenarioTitle: The password nobody wrote down
questions.stem: On the New project form a student clicked `Generate a password`, saw a field full of dots, and moved straight on to the region dropdown without copying anything. Two weeks later they want to connect pgAdmin and are clicking through the dashboard looking for somewhere to read the password back.
options: Open `Project Settings` and click the reveal icon beside the stored database password
It cannot be recovered, only reset under `Database` then `Settings`, which invalidates every saved connection string
Sign in at supabase.com and reuse that account password, since it is the same secret either way
Delete the project and start over, because a lost database password locks you out of the dashboard
optionNotes: There is no reveal button anywhere -- Postgres stores only a hash, and the dashboard itself says the database password is not viewable after creation.
Correct -- reset it in the `Database password` section under `Database` then `Settings`, then expect to re-paste the new one into every tool that had the old one.
These are two different secrets: the account password signs you in to supabase.com, while the database password belongs to the Postgres user named `postgres`.

Losing the database password locks you out of nothing -- your account login is unaffected, and the cost of a reset is re-pasting the new password into your saved connection strings, not any of your data.
questions.takeaway: Copy the generated database password into a password manager before you leave the form, and label it so you never confuse it with your supabase.com login.

questions.scenarioTitle: The quarter-second pause
questions.stem: Sitting in Florida, a student scrolled the `Region` dropdown and picked a Sydney data center because the name looked interesting. Every statement in the SQL Editor now hesitates noticeably before answering, and they want to move the project to `East US (North Virginia)`.
options: Change it under `Project Settings` then `General`, the same place the project name is renamed
Nothing to change -- the region is only a label, so it cannot be what is slowing the queries down
Upgrade to a paid plan, which unlocks moving an existing project to a different region
Create a new project in the closer region and rebuild the data there, since region is fixed at creation
optionNotes: The project name really is renameable there, but the field table on the page marks `Region` as the one choice you cannot change later.
The region is the physical AWS data center your Postgres server lives in, and that distance is exactly what adds the visible round-trip delay to every statement.
A project is bound to its region at the hardware level on every plan, not just the Free one, so paying more does not move it.
Correct -- Supabase's own guidance is to create a new project in the region you want and migrate the data across, which for coursework means building the schema again.
questions.takeaway: Region affects round-trip time only, but it is permanent -- pick the data center nearest you before you click `Create new project`.

questions.scenarioTitle: The repo that was scanned in minutes
questions.stem: A student is about to push their whole course folder to a public GitHub repository. Inside it are a notes file containing the project's database password and a config file holding a key that begins `sb_secret_`. A classmate tells them only one of the two is really sensitive.
options: Neither may be committed -- both grant full control of the database and bypass every Row Level Security rule
Only the database password matters, because API keys are designed to be embedded in code and shared
Both are fine in a file named `.env`, since a filename like that is not indexed by GitHub
Neither matters, because tables built in the SQL Editor are already labelled `Unrestricted` and public
optionNotes: Correct -- the page says both the database password and the `sb_secret_` key grant full control and bypass RLS, and that bots scan public repositories for these strings within minutes of a push.
The safe-to-share key is the `sb_publishable_` one; `sb_secret_` (called `service_role` in older tutorials) is a full-control secret and must stay out of the repository.
A filename hides nothing in a public repository -- every file in it is readable by anyone, and automated scanners read them fast.
`Unrestricted` only means Row Level Security is off, and on projects created on or after 30 May 2026 a new `public` table is invisible to the Data API until you write an explicit `GRANT`.
questions.takeaway: The database password and the `sb_secret_` key are equally dangerous -- keep both out of repositories, chats, screenshots, and homework submissions.

quizzes.heading: Check yourself: running SQL in the Supabase SQL Editor

questions.scenarioTitle: The first query of the semester
questions.stem: A brand-new project has finally stopped saying it is being set up. Before typing any `CREATE TABLE`, a student wants one quick check that the browser really is talking to a live Postgres server. The group chat offers several ways to test it.
options: Run `SHOW DATABASES;` and confirm that a database named `postgres` appears in the list
Open `SQL Editor` and watch a blank `Untitled query` tab appear, since that tab only opens once the database is reachable
Run `SELECT version();` and read the single row whose value begins with the word `PostgreSQL`
Paste the whole `CREATE TABLE REP` script first and treat any red error as a dead connection
optionNotes: `SHOW DATABASES;` is a MySQL habit that does not belong here -- your project already is the database, and it is always named `postgres`.

The blank query tab is just the dashboard's own interface loading; the page warns that a query run too early still fails with a connection error and should be retried in thirty seconds, so the tab proves nothing about the server.
Correct -- `version()` is a built-in PostgreSQL function, and one row in a column headed `version` starting with `PostgreSQL` proves your account, the project, and the database all work.
A red error that quotes your own SQL back at you is a typo, which is a completely different problem from a connection error or a project still provisioning.
questions.takeaway: `SELECT version();` is the smallest statement that proves a database is answering you -- run it before you build anything.

questions.scenarioTitle: The DROP parked at the bottom
questions.stem: A student keeps their entire KimTay script in one query tab, with `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS REP;` sitting at the bottom for later. Wanting to re-run just the three `INSERT` statements, they click into the editor, highlight nothing, and press `Run`.
options: Only the statement the cursor is sitting on runs, so the `DROP` at the bottom is left alone
Everything in the editor runs top to bottom, so the `DROP` runs too once its confirmation dialog is accepted
Nothing runs at all, because the editor requires a highlighted selection before `Run` will do anything
Only the final statement runs, since the editor treats the last semicolon as the end of the script
optionNotes: There is no cursor-line rule in this editor -- it runs your selection, and with nothing selected it runs the entire contents of the box.
Correct -- the page names this as the usual reason a `DROP` you thought was safely parked at the bottom suddenly runs, though Supabase does confirm before destructive statements.
Highlighting is optional, not required: selecting text is how you run only part of a long script, which is the fast way to test one line at a time.
Semicolons tell the editor where one statement stops and the next begins, and all of them run in order -- which is why all three `INSERT` statements can go in a single run.
questions.takeaway: Selection wins: highlight the statements you want, because an empty selection means the whole editor runs, `DROP` included.

questions.scenarioTitle: The table that is not in the list
questions.stem: A student builds `REP` with `CREATE TABLE` in the SQL Editor and gets `Success. No rows returned`. Switching to a tab that already had `Table Editor` open, they see no sign of the table, and a classmate tells them to just rebuild it with the `New table` form instead.
options: Rebuild it with `New table`, since tables created in the SQL Editor never appear in the Table Editor
Nothing was created -- `Success. No rows returned` means the `CREATE TABLE` failed quietly
Search the list for `REP` in capitals, because the Table Editor shows names exactly as they were typed
Reload the page; the Table Editor caches its list, and `rep` is there in lower case
optionNotes: The page says the opposite -- the `rep` table you just built with SQL is already in that list, and the standing advice is build with SQL, browse with the Table Editor.
`Success. No rows returned` is the correct response to a statement that changes the database rather than asking it a question -- the table does exist.
Postgres folds unquoted names to lower case, so `CREATE TABLE REP` stores a table named `rep`; only a double-quoted name keeps its capitals.
Correct -- the page warns that the Table Editor caches the table list and does not always notice a table created in another tab, so reload the page.
questions.takeaway: Build with SQL and browse with the Table Editor -- and remember unquoted names arrive in the list folded to lower case.

matchers.heading: Sort the need into the right place to run SQL
matchers.prompt: Each card describes something a student in this course actually needs. Drop it on the one place from the S-1 table that fits it best -- the throwaway sandbox on this page, a database installed on one computer, or a Supabase project.

cards.text: Try one statement right now with no account, no install, and no waiting
cards.why: The sandbox is the only one of the three with zero setup -- Supabase needs an account and a few minutes of provisioning, and a local install needs downloading.

cards.text: Make a beginner's mistake somewhere it cannot possibly matter, then wipe it with a reload
cards.why: Reloading the page destroys everything in the sandbox, which is exactly what makes it the safest place to get something wrong.

cards.text: Work with no network at all, and still find the same tables waiting next week
cards.why: Only a local install is both offline-capable and permanent: Supabase needs the network, and the sandbox loses your tables at the next reload.

cards.text: Run Module 3's MySQL statements exactly as written, against a database you installed yourself
cards.why: A local install is the only option that can actually be MySQL -- the sandbox is SQLite and Supabase is PostgreSQL.

cards.text: Start an assignment on a lab computer and finish the same tables at home from a browser
cards.why: Supabase stores the data on its own servers, so you sign in from any computer with a browser and pick up exactly where you left off.

cards.text: Keep the KimTay rows safe on a server in case your laptop dies the week work is due
cards.why: The data lives on Supabase's server rather than your hardware, so a dead laptop leaves your `REP` and `CUSTOMER` tables untouched.

quizzes.heading: Check yourself: connecting from a Mac

questions.scenarioTitle: The command that isn't there
questions.stem: A student on a Mac follows the terminal route. `brew install libpq` finishes with no errors, but the very next command, `psql --version`, prints `zsh: command not found: psql`. They have not opened a new Terminal window since the install.
options: Install the full PostgreSQL server with Homebrew, because `libpq` on its own never includes the `psql` program
Reset the Supabase database password, because the client cannot locate the server without fresh credentials
Re-run the `echo ... >> ~/.zshrc` and `source ~/.zshrc` lines, or simply open a brand-new Terminal window
Run the Homebrew installer again, because `command not found` always means Homebrew itself was never installed
optionNotes: `libpq` is the PostgreSQL client package and does provide `psql` without any local database server, which you do not need since your server is Supabase.
This is a local tool problem, not a login problem: the shell never found a program to run, so no password was ever sent anywhere.
Correct - Homebrew installs `libpq` keg-only, so its folder must be added to `PATH` yourself, and a window opened before that edit will not see it.
The error names `psql`, not `brew`; if `brew install` succeeded then Homebrew is fine, and you can confirm the package with `brew list libpq`.
questions.takeaway: `PATH` is the list of folders your shell searches for commands, and a keg-only package is not in it until you add it and reload the shell.

questions.scenarioTitle: Three strings and only one right answer
questions.stem: A student opens the `Connect` panel and sees `Direct connection`, `Transaction pooler`, and `Session pooler`. They are on campus Wi-Fi and want to set up TablePlus on their Mac so they can browse the KimTay tables.
options: The `Session pooler` string, whose host ends in `pooler.supabase.com` and whose port is `5432`
The `Direct connection` string on port `5432`, because it is the shortest path to the database
The `Transaction pooler` string on port `6543`, because pooled connections are always the faster option
Whichever string a tutorial shows, because every Supabase project shares the same pooler host anyway
optionNotes: Correct - both pooler endpoints are reachable over IPv4 on every plan, and session mode behaves like a normal long-lived connection with prepared statements, which is what a desktop client wants.
On a free project the direct connection resolves to an IPv6 address only unless you buy the IPv4 add-on, so on a typical IPv4 network it just hangs and times out.
Transaction mode does not support prepared statements and is meant for serverless and edge functions, not for a desktop SQL client in this course.
Hosts differ by region and by the number after `aws-`, so copying a host from a tutorial is the single most common reason a connection never resolves.
questions.takeaway: For psql, TablePlus, or pgAdmin 4 on a laptop, always copy your own `Session pooler` string on port `5432`.

questions.scenarioTitle: The failure that names the user
questions.stem: A student on a Mac pastes their connection string into psql in Terminal and gets `FATAL: password authentication failed for user postgres.abcdefghijklmnopqrst`. The client clearly reached a server, because the server is the thing complaining.
options: The host name is wrong, because a mistyped host always surfaces later as a password failure
The user name lost its project reference, and the dot must be restored before it can authenticate
Row Level Security is blocking the login until a policy is written for the `postgres` role
The password is wrong, the `[YOUR-PASSWORD]` placeholder is still in the string, or double quotes swallowed a `$`
optionNotes: A wrong host shows up as `could not translate host name ... to address`, and no login is ever attempted because nothing was reached.
Losing the project reference produces the pooler's `Tenant or user not found` message; here the user was recognised, dot and reference included, and only the password was refused.
Row Level Security filters rows inside a session that already exists, and the owner is exempt anyway unless the table was set to `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`.
Correct - those are exactly the three causes the Mac troubleshooting table lists; replace the whole placeholder brackets included, or leave the password out and let `psql` prompt you.
questions.takeaway: Read the error literally: an authentication failure means you reached the right server with the wrong secret, so fix the password, not the host.

quizzes.heading: Check yourself: connecting from Windows

questions.scenarioTitle: The window that remembers too much
questions.stem: On Windows, a classmate runs the EDB installer with `Command Line Tools` checked and confirms `psql.exe` sits in `C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL\18\bin`. They switch back to a PowerShell window they had open all along and get `'psql' is not recognized as the name of a cmdlet`.
options: `PATH` is the folder PostgreSQL installed into, so the fix is reinstalling somewhere with a shorter name
Add `C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL\18\bin` to `Path`, then close every open PowerShell and open a new one
The `PostgreSQL Server` component was left unchecked, so `psql.exe` was never actually installed
Wrap the new `Path` entry in quotation marks and finish it with a backslash so Windows parses it correctly
optionNotes: `PATH` is the list of folders Windows searches for programs, not the install location, so reinstalling elsewhere changes nothing about being found.
Correct - the installer does not add that folder to the path, and a window opened earlier kept the old `PATH`, so a fresh window plus the entry is the fix.
`Command Line Tools` is the component that provides `psql`, and they already confirmed `psql.exe` exists; the server component is optional because the database lives at Supabase.
The entry must have no quotation marks and no trailing backslash, so adding either is how a correct-looking `Path` edit still fails.
questions.takeaway: Prove a `Path` edit worked with `where.exe psql` in a newly opened PowerShell window - never in the window that was already sitting there.

questions.scenarioTitle: The password with punctuation in it
questions.stem: A student's Supabase database password contains a `$` and an `&`. Pasted into PowerShell with no quotation marks, the line never reaches `psql` at all - PowerShell answers `The ampersand (&) character is not allowed`. Wrapped in double quotation marks, the command runs but the connection is refused as an authentication failure instead.
options: Use double quotation marks, because they are the only quotes PowerShell will accept around a connection string
Leave the string unquoted, because PowerShell passes everything after `psql` through to the program untouched
Percent-encode the `$` as `%24` in pgAdmin's `Password` field so both tools finally agree
Wrap the whole connection string in single quotation marks, doubling any single quote that appears inside the password
optionNotes: PowerShell accepts either kind, and double quotes are the trouble: inside them anything starting with `$` is expanded, which is why the password silently arrived wrong.
Unquoted, `&` is reserved and produces that error, `;` ends the command, `#` starts a comment, and a space splits the argument in two.

Two mistakes at once: pgAdmin's `Password` field is not a URL and takes the password literally, and the characters this section has you percent-encode are `@ : / ? # [ ] %` - the fix for `$` is quoting, not encoding.
Correct - single quotes stop `$` expansion and neutralise `&`, `;`, `#`, and spaces; a literal single quote inside is written twice.
questions.takeaway: Single quotes in PowerShell, every time - or skip the URL entirely with the `-h -p -d -U` flag form and type the password at the prompt.

questions.scenarioTitle: The tree with nothing in it
questions.stem: A student opens pgAdmin 4 for the first time on the lab computer. The `Object Explorer` on the left shows only a `Servers` node with nothing under it, and their connection string is sitting in Notepad next to the window.
options: Right-click `Servers`, choose `Register` then `Server...`, and fill the `Connection` tab from the string
Paste the whole `postgresql://...` string into the `Host name/address` box on the `Connection` tab
Type the database name `postgres` into `Name` on the `General` tab so pgAdmin knows which database to open
Type the pgAdmin master password into `Password`, because that is the credential pgAdmin uses to reach Supabase
optionNotes: Correct - that is the path (some builds read `Create` then `Server...`), and the host, port, maintenance database, username, and password all come out of the one string.
pgAdmin wants the pieces separately: the host is only what sits between `@` and the last `:`, such as `aws-1-us-east-1.pooler.supabase.com`.
`Name` on the `General` tab is just a label for you with no effect on the connection; the database name goes in `Maintenance database` on the `Connection` tab.
The master password only protects saved server passwords on that computer; the `Password` field needs your Supabase database password, typed literally.
questions.takeaway: Registering a server is just the connection string taken apart into five labelled boxes, and pgAdmin's labels differ slightly from the words in the string.

matchers.heading: Match the Windows error to what actually caused it
matchers.prompt: Every message below is one a Windows student in this section really hits: PowerShell, psql, or pgAdmin refusing to cooperate. Drop each card into the bucket that names its cause. Read the whole card - the detail buried at the end, not the first few words, is what decides the answer.

zones.label: The tool is not on PATH

cards.text: `'psql' is not recognized as the name of a cmdlet` in a PowerShell window that was already open before the `Path` entry was added
cards.why: That window captured the old `PATH`; close every PowerShell and Command Prompt, open a fresh one, and prove the edit with `where.exe psql`.

cards.text: `where.exe psql` prints nothing at all, and the `Path` entry was pasted as `"C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL\18\bin\"`
cards.why: A `Path` entry takes no quotation marks and no trailing backslash, so this one never resolves - re-enter it plainly and check that the version number matches the folder you actually have.

cards.text: `psql: error: connection to server ... FATAL: Tenant or user not found` comes back the instant PowerShell runs the line
cards.why: That message comes from the pooler, not from PostgreSQL: the user must read `postgres.` plus your project reference, so re-copy the whole string from the `Connect` panel instead of editing the old one.

cards.text: `could not connect to server: Connection timed out` after a long wait, from a string whose host starts with `db.` and ends in `supabase.co`
cards.why: The direct connection resolves to IPv6 only without the paid IPv4 add-on - use the session-mode pooler string, and if that still hangs, test on a phone hotspot to see whether the school network is blocking outbound 5432.

cards.text: The password prompt keeps repeating, and the password itself contains `@` and `#` typed straight into the connection string
cards.why: Those characters are structural in a URL, so percent-encode them (`%40`, `%23`) inside the string, or switch to the `-h -p -d -U` flag form and type the password at the prompt.

cards.text: The same password is accepted in pgAdmin every time but rejected in PowerShell whenever the connection string is wrapped in double quotation marks
cards.why: Inside double quotes PowerShell expands anything starting with `$`, so the password silently arrives changed; single quotation marks send it exactly as typed.

cards.text: pgAdmin reports `could not translate host name ... to address` for a host that was retyped by hand and still ends in `pooler.supabase.com`
cards.why: The endpoint choice was right but a character is wrong - re-copy the host from your own `Connect` panel rather than retyping it, and make sure no `[` or `]` survived in any field.

quizzes.heading: Check yourself: porting Module 3 SQL to Postgres

questions.scenarioTitle: The whole-script paste
questions.stem: A student opens the Module 3 `.sql` script, selects all of it, and pastes it straight into the Supabase SQL Editor. Before pressing Run they stop and ask what actually has to be edited. According to this section, what is the honest edit list?
options: Rewrite every `SELECT`, join and `WHERE` clause, because Postgres uses a different query language than MySQL
Leave `CREATE DATABASE KimTay;` and `USE KimTay;` at the top -- Postgres quietly ignores lines it does not need
Delete the `CREATE DATABASE` and `USE` lines, drop the backticks, and add one `ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` per table
Replace every `CHAR`, `VARCHAR` and `DECIMAL` column with a Postgres-only type name before anything will run
optionNotes: MySQL and Postgres both speak standard SQL, so the query work from Module 3 carries over character for character.
Creating the Supabase project already created the database, and your connection points straight at it, so both lines come out and the script starts at `CREATE TABLE`.
Correct -- the section summarizes the port as exactly this: delete two lines at the top, drop the backticks, add one `ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;` per table, keep the rest.
Every type KimTay uses -- `CHAR`, `VARCHAR`, `DECIMAL`, `DATE`, `SMALLINT` -- exists in Postgres under the same name and needs no edit.
questions.takeaway: Porting the Module 3 script is a short edit list at the edges, not a rewrite of your SQL.

questions.scenarioTitle: The table that exists but cannot be found
questions.stem: A student creates their table with `CREATE TABLE "REP" ("REP_NUM" CHAR(2));` because the Module 3 script used capitals everywhere. The Table Editor shows a table called `REP`. Then `SELECT * FROM REP;` fails with `relation "rep" does not exist`. What happened?
options: The double quotes locked the name in as uppercase `REP`, while the unquoted query folded to lowercase and missed it
Postgres is case-sensitive about everything, so retyping the query in capitals as `SELECT * FROM REP;` will find the table
The table was never really created, because Postgres rejects any `CREATE TABLE` whose name is wrapped in double quotes
Supabase hides a new table from the SQL Editor until Row Level Security has been enabled on it
optionNotes: Correct -- a quoted identifier keeps its case exactly, an unquoted one folds to lowercase, so the query looked for `rep` and the table is genuinely `REP`; the repair is `ALTER TABLE "REP" RENAME TO rep;`.
The query already was in capitals -- Postgres folded it down to `rep` anyway, which is precisely why it failed.
The `CREATE TABLE` succeeded; the Table Editor is listing the table, which is the proof that quoting created it rather than blocking it.
RLS controls the auto-generated web API, not the SQL Editor -- your own SQL Editor queries keep working with RLS on and no policy.
questions.takeaway: Never put double quotes around a table or column name when you create it; type it unquoted and lowercase.

questions.scenarioTitle: There is no DESCRIBE here
questions.stem: A student needs to check the columns, types and NOT NULL settings of `rep` for a homework answer. They are working entirely in the browser and have nothing installed on the lab computer. What does this section tell them to do?
options: Type `\d rep` into the Supabase SQL Editor, since that is the standard Postgres replacement for `DESCRIBE`
Run `DESCRIBE rep;` in the SQL Editor -- it is standard SQL and behaves the same in every database
Query `information_schema.columns` for `table_name = 'REP'`, matching the uppercase name typed at creation
Click `rep` in the Table Editor, or query `information_schema.columns` with `table_schema = 'public'` and `table_name = 'rep'`
optionNotes: `\d` is a `psql` meta-command, never sent to the server, and typing it in the browser editor gives `syntax error at or near "\"`.
`DESCRIBE` is a MySQL statement that does not exist in Postgres, so it is not standard SQL and will not run here.
`information_schema` stores the folded lowercase name, so searching for `'REP'` returns zero rows -- a confusing way to be told your table exists.
Correct -- these are the two options the section gives you in the browser: the Table Editor, and that `information_schema.columns` query with both values lowercase and in single quotes.
questions.takeaway: `DESCRIBE` does not exist in Postgres -- in the browser, use the Table Editor or an `information_schema.columns` query.

questions.scenarioTitle: The lines nobody had to touch
questions.stem: Two classmates are arguing over a printout of the Module 3 script, marking which lines survive the move to Postgres untouched. One of them is right about a whole group of lines. Which claim matches what this section says does NOT change?
options: `LIMIT 20, 10` moves across unchanged, because both products accept the comma form of paging
Joins, `GROUP BY`, `COUNT`, `IS NULL` and the KimTay `CHAR` / `VARCHAR` / `DECIMAL` / `DATE` columns are identical
`AUTO_INCREMENT` carries over, because auto-numbering is part of the SQL standard both products implement
Double quotes still work around text such as `"Kaiser"`, exactly as they did under MySQL's default settings
optionNotes: Postgres rejects the comma form; only `LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20` works there, so this line is one of the few that must be edited.

Correct -- the section calls the query keywords, aggregates and joins identical character for character, and says the KimTay column types exist under the same names with no edits needed; everything conceptual from Module 2 carries over too.
`AUTO_INCREMENT` is a MySQL-only keyword and Postgres answers `syntax error at or near "AUTO_INCREMENT"`; the standard spelling is `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY`.
In Postgres double quotes always mean a table or column name, so this gives `column "Kaiser" does not exist` -- text needs single quotes.
questions.takeaway: Almost all of your Module 3 querying, and all of Module 2's design thinking, transfers to Postgres unchanged.

quizzes.heading: Check yourself: keys, leaks and backups

questions.scenarioTitle: The key that ships to the browser
questions.stem: A classmate is building a small web page that lists KimTay items, and the page's JavaScript is downloaded by anyone who visits. They have three strings from the dashboard in front of them and ask which one belongs in that JavaScript. Which credential is designed for this?
options: The database password, because the page has to log in to Postgres somehow before it can read any rows
The publishable key (`sb_publishable_...`, or the `anon` key on an older project), whose access Row Level Security decides
The secret key (`sb_secret_...`), because it is the only one guaranteed to return rows on every request
Any of the three is fine as long as the repository is private and Row Level Security is switched on
optionNotes: The database password belongs in your connection tool and nowhere else -- it is for `psql`, pgAdmin or TablePlus, never for code a user can see.
Correct -- the publishable key is a public, low-privilege key that identifies your project, and the table says it is the only one designed to be shipped in a browser app.
It returns rows every time precisely because it bypasses Row Level Security entirely, which is why it must never appear in browser code, a public repo, or a screenshot.
A private repository is not protection: browser JavaScript is downloaded by every visitor, so whatever is in it is public regardless of where the source lives.
questions.takeaway: Exactly one Supabase credential is meant to be public: the publishable / `anon` key.

questions.scenarioTitle: The connection string in the class chat
questions.stem: A student cannot get `psql` to connect, so they paste their whole session pooler connection string -- real password included -- into the class group chat asking what is wrong. Ten minutes later they realize what they have done. What is the fix?
options: Delete the chat message; once it is gone, nobody can use that password any more
Nothing needs doing, because a connection string only works from the machine that first generated it
Ask Supabase support to display the old password so it can be compared against what leaked
Reset the password at `Database` -> `Settings`, rebuild the connection string, update every saved tool, then delete the message
optionNotes: Deleting the message does not un-see it -- the section says there is no undo for a leaked secret, and the old password keeps working until it is replaced.
A Postgres connection string is not tied to one computer, which is exactly why the section treats a pasted string as compromised.
Supabase shows the database password once when you create the project and never displays it again, so nobody can read it back to you -- the only move is a reset.

Correct -- this is the rotation sequence in the section: reset the password, wait a moment, rebuild the string from `Connect` replacing `[YOUR-PASSWORD]`, update pgAdmin/TablePlus/`.env`, then clean up the leak.
questions.takeaway: Rotating the secret is what makes a leak harmless; deleting the message is only the last step.

questions.scenarioTitle: The night before it is due
questions.stem: A student wants to be sure that a broken project, a paused project, or a Supabase login problem cannot cost them their graded KimTay work. They list four things they could call a backup. Which one is the real backup this section describes?
options: A plain text `.sql` file you keep in your own notes, holding every `CREATE TABLE` and `INSERT` in run order
The project on Supabase itself, since a paused project stays restorable from the dashboard for up to a year
A screenshot of the Table Editor showing every row currently in `REP` and `CUSTOMER`
The second Supabase project you created to test the script, now that it holds the same tables
optionNotes: Correct -- the section calls that file your backup, your rebuild script and your submission at once, and tells you to prove it by running it against an empty project.

matchers.heading: Translate it: MySQL line to Postgres equivalent
matchers.prompt: Each card is something you wrote in Module 3 under MySQL. Drop it on the Supabase Postgres equivalent from this section's translation sheet.

zones.label: Nothing -- delete both lines
zones.hint: Your project already is the database

cards.text: `CREATE DATABASE KimTay;` followed by `USE KimTay;` at the top of the script
cards.why: Creating the Supabase project created the database, so both lines come out and the script starts at `CREATE TABLE`.

cards.text: `DESCRIBE REP;` to see the columns, types and NOT NULL settings
cards.why: `DESCRIBE` does not exist in Postgres; click the table in the Table Editor or query `information_schema.columns`.

cards.text: `SHOW TABLES;` to list everything in the current database
cards.why: The Table Editor sidebar lists your tables, or you can query `information_schema.tables` for the same answer.

cards.text: `ID INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY` on a table of your own
cards.why: `AUTO_INCREMENT` is a MySQL-only keyword that Postgres rejects with a syntax error; the standard spelling is `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY`.

cards.text: A `CREATE TABLE` whose table and column names are each wrapped in MySQL backticks
cards.why: Postgres does not use backticks at all -- remove them and do not replace them with double quotes, so the names fold to lowercase.

cards.text: `INSERT INTO REP ... VALUES ("Kaiser", "Valerie");` which MySQL accepted
cards.why: In Postgres double quotes name a column, so this gives `column "Kaiser" does not exist`; text values take single quotes.

matchers.heading: Sort it: where is this allowed to appear?
matchers.prompt: Drop each item on the only place this section says it may safely live.

zones.label: Anywhere -- it holds no credential
zones.hint: SQL statements only, no key inside

cards.text: The publishable key that starts with `sb_publishable_`
cards.why: It is a public, low-privilege credential whose access Row Level Security decides -- the only one designed to ship in a browser app.

cards.text: The `anon` key on the `Legacy API keys` tab of an older project
cards.why: `anon` is the old name for the publishable key, so the same rule applies: the low-privilege credential is the public one.

cards.text: The secret key that starts with `sb_secret_`
cards.why: It bypasses Row Level Security completely, so it belongs only in code on a server you control, read from an uncommitted environment variable.

cards.text: The `service_role` JWT copied from an older project
cards.why: `service_role` is the old name for the secret key -- same power, same rule: never in a browser app, a public repo, or a screenshot.

cards.text: The database password for the Postgres `postgres` user
cards.why: It is the value you paste into a connection string for `psql`, pgAdmin or TablePlus, and the section says it belongs nowhere else.

cards.text: `kimtay-setup.sql` containing only `CREATE TABLE` and `INSERT` statements
cards.why: It holds SQL only -- no password, no connection string, no key -- so the section says it is safe to email yourself, drop in cloud storage, or commit.
